speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in introducing this Bill for third reading I would like to make some observations that were not permitted during the report stage, and to clear up some of the confusion that has been generated in previous debate.
I would like to remind the House of the purpose of Bill C-55. The combined effect of these amendments is to allow the 1AB to do more work, to be more efficient, and to retain effectiveness in the face of a mounting queue of appeals. The Bill will also equalize appeal rights between citizens and permanent residents of Canada.
Through the debate it was evident that some Members opposite feel that Bill C-55 is designed to eliminate the refugee claims backlog or pre-empt Parliament's options for a new determination system. Mr. Speaker, the Bill will do neither.
The IAB has a backlog in immigration appeals and in refugee determinations of greater proportion than can be managed by 32 new Members. This capacity, however, will allow the Board to reduce the immigration appeal backlog and prevent further growth until a new and simpler system is legislated and put into effect. Not to do this would deprive many people of an opportunity for a hearing within a reasonable time, and would be an invitation to even greater abuse of the claims process than is now taking place.
In regard to pre-empting the form of a new system, 1 can only reaffirm that the options remain open. The fact that these appointments are being made to the IAB signifies only that for the time being we must work within the existing system. The new appointments are short term so that in future we will have choices regarding the housing of a new system without being constrained by the existance of a large ongoing organization. The fact that we are adding more capacity to the IAB will not satisfy those Members opposite who think an amnesty is the only thing to do. However, it will satisfy the broader community who wish to see our compassion dispensed with due regard to merit. I hope all Members will therefore join with the Government in giving speedy passage to this Bill.
The Bill proposes several amendments to the Immigration Act. They are minor in nature and designed to increase the flexibility and capacity of the IAB to deal with a greater number of cases. Under the current Act the maximum number of Board members is 18. We realize that with one as chairman and the guideline of three members per hearing, we have the option of five teams to do the work. This Bill would increase the maximum number of members to 50. The Board reviews appeals of family class applications which have been refused abroad. It hears appeals against deportation orders by certain people who have come to Canada and have not been admitted or who, having been admitted, have run afoul of the Immigration Act. The Board also makes a redetermination of refugee claims which have been evaluated by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee but subsequently rejected by the Minister.
All of these categories of cases are important, but the Board has far more work than it can do. This Bill will permit the Board to appoint new members as needed, for two-year terms, with the possibility of one extension depending on the workload. In addition, the number of vice-chairman will be increased from five to 13, giving the Board even greater flexibility. The Bill would also require that not fewer than half the vice-chairman be members of a provincial bar for at least five years. To ensure that Board members are used effectively, the Bill would permit the chairman to delegate responsibility on technical matters to one-member panels and, on more serious matters, when the parties consent, to a single-member hearing.
The Supreme Court of Canada ruled in the Singh case that all refugees before the IAB were entitled to an oral hearing. The effect of this decision is to lengthen the already long line of people awaiting hearing before the Immigration Appeal Board. The increase in membership will permit more redeterminations and thereby respond to the Supreme Court's ruling.
In addition to the refugee claims' backlog there are also more than 1,000 family sponsorship appeals pending. Families which cannot be reunited because of a legal prohibition must wait more than a year to determine whether relief may be
February 25, 1986

possible. Some of these cases involve the parents of Canadians for whom delay cannot be sustained. Bill C-55 goes farther than simply reducing the delay for these people. It extends the right of appeal to permanent residents as well as Canadian citizens. The right of appeal has always been available only to sponsors who are Canadian citizens. In our view that is not consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Therefore, this Bill will grant the right of appeal to permanent residents as well as Canadian citizens. I represent a community which is 50 per cent ethnic in nature. The City of Saint Laurent, one of our important cities, has some 68,000 people, and 50 per cent of those are members of cultural minorities, all of them immigrants to Canada. We know the great challenge people face when they give up everything in their homeland to come to a new country, quite often with only the shirts on their backs, and then be faced with lengthy delays in the immigration process. So, it is really a proud moment for me to be able to participate in a process which will speed up this whole operation and once and for all help clean up the backlog.
As I tried to state very clearly, this Bill does not pre-empt what will be done in future legislation dealing with the refugee determination process. We are trying to correct an existing situation and allow new legislation to cover the refugee experience in days to come. I hope all Members of this House will give speedy passage to this Bill on third reading so that the IAB can continue its effective work in days to come.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, is a Bill which the Minister responsible has said, in this House and in Vancouver recently, would go far to correct some of the problems faced by the Immigration Appeal Board. There is nothing wrong with the Bill in that it certainly will do something. However, it will not do what the Government claims it will do. Perhaps I can give an example to show exactly what I mean and impress upon the Government the necessity of some urgent action in this regard.
I have heard Members in this Chamber, especially Conservatives, whenever I have said anything about immigration, say to me: "Well, how many immigration appeal cases have you had?" or: "What do you know about immigration?" I must admit that I do not deal with as many cases as some Members from central Canada or other provinces. However, I can tell you that in my home community of Gander, Newfoundland, over 100 people a year depart from aircraft arriving from the Soviet Union, East Germany, Cuba or other East bloc countries, to claim political asylum. When I look at this Bill I see that it will only take care of that number of people who get off those aircraft in Gander, Newfoundland, that is all.
The Government says it is going to address a problem. What is the problem? The problem is a clogging of the system of appeals before the IAB. This Bill increases the size of that Board. It does what a judge in a Canadian court said should be done with respect to oral hearings. However, all it does is to take care of an extra 100 or 200 appeals a year. In other
Immigration Act, 1976
words, it will take care of Gander, Newfoundland, but it is not addressing the problem.
No one knows the exact number for sure, but there are over 15,000 people claiming refugee status who have to be dealt with by the IAB. Under the family sponsorship appeal program there is an additional 1,500 or so waiting to be heard. Those numbers are increasing daily, yet the Government of Canada has the audacity to come into this Chamber and say that by dealing with this Act to amend the Immigration Act we will over the next two or three months increase the size of the IAB, and effect other changes. To do what? To correct the problem that we have in Canada today with appeals under the Immigration Act.
As I say, there is not much wrong with the Bill, but there is not very much right with it either when you look at the size of the problem that we have in Canada today. It does not address the major problem of the backlog. It does not do other things that have to be addressed by this Government. It does not do anything to address the unfairness of the immigration system that we have in the country.
You could have a case of somebody who wants to bring over a family member from some other country. That sponsor may have had that appeal before the Board for a couple of years, and perhaps there is a stalling tactic at the other end for those family members. I can cite for you a case where a gentleman wanted to bring over his father and his sister. For five years that case was stalled until finally the father died. The sister, by this time, had reached the age of 21. Then, of course, sponsorship went right out the window. For five years that was held up. Now, granted, it wasn't solely the responsibility of the Appeal Board because they had a problem on the other end.
Let us consider the case of somebody who gets on a plane in one country and is perhaps briefed on what to say, or the answers to give to the questionnaire that he is given when he arrives in Canada claiming refugee status. On the basis solely of that questionnaire his or her answers to the questions determine whether or not that person will be successful in being able to remain in Canada. Then I compare that to the other case where somebody waits for five years and does not make it in the end anyway. You can see a tremendous unfairness within the system. The Bill does not address that either.
What does the Bill address? It does not address the backlog, it does not address the unfairness in the system. It does not address the fact that Canada is now seen as the place people who know the system and are able to work it can be successful in getting into this country. There are many who should be allowed into this country but are not successful. I do not know what else to say about the Bill except that it does not do very much; it does nothing.
A band-aid.
The Hon. Member said a band-aid. You could call it a band-aid, but there are different sizes of band-aids.

A small.

February 25, 1986
Immigration Act, 1976

There are very large ones, small ones, medium ones, so I suppose this is a strip off the small one. But 1 cannot see any other good that it does. Yet the Government of Canada has this incredible problem which was created over the past year and is not doing a thing about it. Some 25,000 people are held in limbo. I suppose this is because we are a signatory to the United Nations agreement, but to do nothing about the problem is absolutely ridiculous.
I do not know what the Government intends to do. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary said: "Well, this is not the ultimate solution because the Government of Canada is going to do something." It is going to take some action". What we want to know is when the Government of Canada is going to take some action. What is it going to do? How is it going to relieve the unfairness in the present system which has come to light over the past year, since this Government took office? I suppose that is all one can say about it, it doesn't do anything at all. Perhaps it helps 100 or 150 extra cases a year, enough to take care of Gander, Newfoundland, but it does not address the problem at all.

Mr. Speaker, I rise, in the absence of the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), to join in this debate on Bill C-55. I have been listening with interest to the Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) addressing this matter and describing the Bill in various ways. I may characterize the Bill somewhat differently from his characterization, but certainly it is a fine question in terms of timing and the value of this Bill to decide exactly how to characterize it.
I note that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976, was given first reading in the House on June 19, 1985. It comes to us now for third reading late in February of 1986. In the interim a number of important things have happened. One of those has been the report of Rabbi Plaut on the question of refugee determination.
This is certainly a very serious problem that faces the Government of Canada, a matter of very great concern to many Canadians and a matter that is of interest to every Canadian in terms of our undertanding of Canada's place in the world in providing a place where refugees can find a refuge which preserves their lives and allows them to re-establish family and property. If they have to lose everything except their lives somewhere else, they should be able to make something of themselves in the large spaces, and I trust the friendly climes of this country.
The matter of refugee determination is an enormously important one which this Bill is surely designed, in the Government's mind, to address. That is precisely the difficulty that faces us, because Rabbi Plaut's report has not been the only one which dealt in a humane and compassionate way with the difficulties that face persons who regard themselves as refugees from one country or another.
This Bill comes before us now for third reading after the Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration has considered it and provided in its fifth report, tabled in the House last November on November 7, a range of recommendations designed to furnish the Government of Canada with means to deal in a compassionate way with the matter of refugee determination.
The Government has 120 sitting days in the House to respond to that report. So we continue to wait. The Government has almost until the end of April to provide its response to that report of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. I am concerned about what the Government's response will be. If the Government tells us in the next couple of months that the action taken as a result of Bill C-55 is adequate to deal with the enormous administrative and human problem of refugee determination, we will know that it has failed to fulfil its obligation to provide compassion in the administration of Government. That is why we are awaiting the response of the Government about a new structure of refugee determination. I fear that the changes to the Immigration Appeal Board we are considering may be the Government's view of an adequate response. If so, it has failed the people of Canada and will have lost a place in the honourable traditions of this country.
We recognize that the present Immigration Appeal Board is hard pressed and that an increase in its number is in order. In fact, the Hon. Member for Spadina has proposed an increase to 36 to allow the board to expand its activities and meet other immigration appeal needs that exist. However, we are concerned that increasing the personnel to 50 in order to take care of all cases may be a temptation not to establish the kind of refugee board that is called for.
It is of great human importance that a review board be established to provide a different approach to the problem and allow for procedures that are not adversarial, as they are with the Immigration Appeal Board. We must not have an appeal structure that continues the full adversarial traditions that govern our law courts with their ancient Anglo-Saxon roots of trial by ordeal. We are dealing with refugees who often come from societies where they have been attacked and suppressed by authorities in their countries after being involved in struggles for human rights and social justice against repressive regimes. The Government must establish a refugee board whose procedures make it possible for those claiming refugee status to present their case in a non-adversarial setting. It could be in the nature of an interview by a couple of people who listen carefully and exemplify the kind of compassionate approach to refugees for which Canada takes pride. The Government will have failed completely if it does not establish such a refugee board and only proceeds with an increased Immigration Appeal Board with its adversarial setting.
I suggest that the Bill is useful only if it provides additional resources for an immigration appeal process which has been overloaded with cases that should have been dealt with long ago, given the enormous backlog. Obviously, we have no objection to expanding the Immigration Appeal Board to 36 in order to ensure that those cases not involving refugee status are dealt with more expeditiously. However, the concern
February 25, 1986

remains that this will be a small response to very large problems. Since we are still awaiting a response from the Government, we are not assured that it will establish a refugee board with different procedures that will ensure a relaxed atmosphere and humane consideration for the situation facing people who have come to Canada from many parts of the world.
There is another disturbing aspect to the establishment of a larger Immigration Appeal Board. In order for the new appointees to deal immmediately with the backlog they will have to immerse themselves in the subject and learn a great deal to provide proper adjudication of these matters. There are questions about the advisability of appeal board members becoming specialists. However, this is likely to happen with the striking of sub-boards or splitting up the board to hear cases. The expanded Immigration Appeal Board will not be able to fulfil its responsibility of dealing with refugee claimants in the fair and humane way that Canadians expect of those appointees.
There are numerous reasons why I hesitate to call this a good Bill. I might call it a good Bill if I was assured that the Government plans to take the action recommended in the fifth report of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. Then one could regard this Bill as simply an improvement to the ability of the Immigration Appeal Board to hear cases. However, we will only know how to regard this Bill with the passage of time, when we know whether the Government plans to develop the institutions that are required to live up to our tradition of compassion and openness to refugees.
I make those reservations because of our experience with another bill coming from the Department of Employment and Immigration dealing with employment equity. One could not regard the provisions of that Bill as objectionable if they are part of a genuine Employment equity bill. The provisions of that Bill provide for reporting, suggest that standards be established and arouse hope that there will be progress made by employers. However, practically everyone in the country who is genuinely concerned about the achievement of employment equity in Government and business across the country is convinced that there should be a timetable and well formulated plans as well as an adequately established and financed enforcement mechanism to ensure that employment equity will in fact be achieved.
After weeks of consideration of that Bill in the committee and in the House, it does not appear that the Government plans to move any further than that quite truncated Employment Equity Bill. As my Party's critic for multiculturalism, having seen the Government fail in the development of employment equity in this area, I am concerned that this Bill to expend the Immigration Appeal Board to deal with the backlog of cases will continue to be the mechanism for those seeking refugee status to present their cases and that the adversarial procedure will continue to be the norm. The officers who seem by their practice to think it is more important to exclude people from Canada than it is to provide refuge in this
Immigration Act, 1976
country will continue their work. Those manifestations of a mean spirit which one sees in a Conservative Government at various times will continue to be exemplified in this area unless we are fortunate to have a Government which acts responsibly. I should not call that "fortunate", should I? We expect responsible Government and we expect a compassionate Government in this area. Later this year we hope to see the Government present a Bill to establish the refugee determination board, or whatever it may be called, which provides for those non-adversarial procedures which will ensure that those frightened people, those people who were tortured in their country and still bear the wounds of this oppression in their minds and spirits and in their very bodies, will have a fair, generous, open and compassionate opportunity to have their refugee status established. If that happens, then I will be prepared that day to look back for a moment and say that Bill C-55, which deals with other matters as well as with the backlog which does require additional resources, and with 50 members rather than 36 members, was probably a good Bill. In the meantime, I suspend judgement on this Bill. However, out of a concern that a penny-pinching Government is not going to do that, I will in fact be voting, even if only on division, against this Bill. I fear that the Government is not going to act.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member who just spoke if he agrees with his colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), who spoke on this subject yesterday? He said quite forthrightly that Immigration officers were making decisions in overseas posts by way of their friendship with dictators in those lands. Would the Hon. Member agree with his colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, with that spurious allegation?

Mr. Speaker, 1 do not have the knowledge which would allow me to agree or disagree, so I probably cannot provide any satisfying response to the Hon. Member. Perhaps I could say that I hope to God that is not true. I hope to God that for the sake of this country, which values its land as a place where refugees can find escape from the oppressive regimes which tarnish the face of the globe, no Canadian officers anywhere in the world would be involved in anything of that sort. Perhaps that indicates where my heart lies. The information is not in my hands.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak very briefly on Bill C-55 this morning and perhaps take the opportunity at the same time to say a few words on the whole immigration issue. I am a new Member of the House of Commons and I am not located in a riding where a large number of immigrants live. Nevertheless, as we all do, I get a number of immigration cases and I cannot help but get the feeling of how unfair the present system is with its built in unexcusable delays. There are cases of constituents who come to see us and tell us that their spouses have been deported. Sometimes the people have been married for years, and the

February 25, 1986
Immigration Act, 1976
spouse has to leave the country and reapply to come back in order to join their loved ones.
One of my constituents has been waiting two years for her husband, who is now in India, to be able to apply to come back to Canada. Her husband had been here on a student visa. They got married and he lived here for some years with his wife. He then had to leave the country in order to reapply to come back. Of course if one was in the country illegally at that time, one would expect that that person would have to rectify whatever was inadequate on one's dossier, to start with. However, that being said, to cause a family to be separated for years in order to accommodate a shuffling of papers hardly seems fair to me.
An individual who had been sponsoring his sister to come into this country phoned me last year. The difficulty in this particular situation was that, although the individual had filled out the proper documentation, the young woman at the other end who was applying to leave had to obtain an exit visa from that particular regime. By the time she received the exit visa the application filled out by her brother had already elapsed. The Canadian applicant applied again to have his sister allowed to come here, but by the time his new application had been processed the exit visa for the sister had expired. Any system which creates that sort of difficulty for no logical reason cannot be considered as fair.
Bill C-55, in a very small way, as the Parliamentary Secretary indicated, hopes to address some of the issues involving backlogs but, obviously, it is not going to correct the situation 1 have just described. In our offices abroad there are such backlogs in processing applications that the resultant delays are causing a complete denial of justice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: That's unfair.
Does the Hon. Member opposite want the floor?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: It's very unfair.

If the Hon. Member wants the floor, I am perfectly willing to let him ask questions later. Perhaps he can start writing one out now and he will have finished the first line in the next half hour. Meanwhile, I will continue to speak on behalf of my constituents, whether he likes it or not.
There are other immigration issues with which I have had to deal in my constituency which are equally unfair. As you know, Mr. Speaker, because you do travel extensively through the riding I have the honour to represent, my constituency is largely rural. Of course, many farmers do apply to have people come into this country to work on their farms. Some of them, of course, are only temporary workers and that would not involve the discussion at hand here. What is of concern to me the people who come into this country to work on a permanent basis on Canadian farms. There are many decisions made which are equally unfair, and I would like the Parliamentary Secretary to take note of some of these problems. Hopefully at some point in the future they will be corrected for the benefit of those people I represent.
There is the case of a farmer in his sixties who had a person from Holland come to work on his farm. This was part of the student exchange program. The young person who came from Holland was a graduate in various sectors of agriculture, principally dairy production and other related fields involving the raising and production of dairy products. He had a proficiency and knowledge of such issues as artificial insemination, the records of production of dairy cattle and so on. This particular person was highly qualified in this field.
Unfortunately, in this particular case the farmer became very ill and had to be hospitalized for some time. He applied for permission to have this individual stay in the country for a longer period of time because without him to run his farm it would cease to operate. He obtained a short extension. However, the farmer, not being in any better state of health after some period of time, was in a situation in which he wanted this individual who came from the same country from which he had come to remain on his farm on a permanent basis. He was told by people in the Department that that could not be done on a permanent basis because in their view there were ample Canadians qualified to perform this type of work. So the farmer placed an ad in the newspapers, as he was required to do, in order to find a Canadian who had the knowledge for which he was looking. No one applied. I should not say no one applied because apparently at one point in time one individual did apply. The applicant had been working in the bush or something like that and had absolutely no knowledge of farming. He had no knowledge of modern technology or farm machinery.
There are those in the Department who evaluate these types of situations who are still of the opinion, unfortunately, that people working on farms are not too qualified and that anybody could do the work. They felt my constituent had been unreasonable in not accepting the person who was not qualified. All this to say that at one point immigration officials wanted to deport this individual. By so doing they would have effectively shut down a very large dairy farm in my constituency since there was absolutely no one left to run it. It was even quite difficult to find someone just to assist the farmer in taking care of his farm operations. It was definitely not possible to find someone of the proper calibre and with the proper experience to actually manage the farm operation. I see an Hon. Member sitting across the way who has some knowledge of agriculture. I am sure he would agree that we want people in agriculture who are not only well meaning but who have some knowledge of what they are doing, such as the farmers we have in my constituency.
In this particular case I had to make representation all the way up to the Minister to obtain a temporary extension to have this individual stay for another short period of time. It was eventually granted. It would have been completely outrageous had it not been granted. However, one cannot help but wonder in cases such as this why it is necessary to have dozens of interventions, interviews, refusals, appeals and more appeals to the Minister in order to obtain what was only just and
February 25, 1986

equitable to start with and which most reasonable people should have been able to recognize the very first day. It was very difficult to convince the authorities that, indeed, this was the proper decision.
The unusual thing about this situation is that the whole process involving my constituent was taking place at the same time as I was hearing cabinet Ministers in the House making long-winded speeches about how we should be increasing our immigration targets. They were telling us that they wanted to increase immigration targets, at the same time as they wanted to deport some people who were working in my constituency, people who we could not do without in terms of the needs felt by the farming community.
So I say to the Parliamentary Secretary that although a large number of the issues I have raised have nothing to do with the number of judges sitting on the Appeal Board, they nevertheless have to do with the whole malaise which exists within the immigration system in Canada. I hope that he will take note of these few points.
Some of the situations have been with us for many years and some have even gotten worse over the last year or two, as has been pointed out by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker). However, whether these inequitable situations have existed for six months or six years, the fact remains that they need to be rectified and addressed as soon as possible by all Members of Parliament. They are not issues on which we want to be separated along Party lines. I think we will want the system to be fair.
I believe all Parties have indicated their willingness to agree with the new quotas which the Minister has recently indicated. We all want the process to work. There is no disagreement among Members on all sides of the House that it be approved. What is needed now is the willingness and desire to put the machinery in place in order to sort out the areas in which we have huge backlogs. Bill C-55 identifies one small area. However, there are others, such as the people in our offices abroad who require far greater attention in terms of taking care of the backlogs.
To summarize, 1 believe there is a willingness on the part of all Members, and it is my hope that there is a willingness on the part of the Government, the Minister, the Parliamentary Secretary and the officials in the Department, to take note of some the things about which we are talking today in the hope of correcting inequitites which exist in the system, both in terms of the representation in the appeal process and elsewhere where the system is deficient.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member. I know he is new in the House and does not have too many immigration cases in his constituency. There are a couple of things I would like to point out to him, especially since immigration is probably one of the largest constituency problems I deal with in my riding of Brampton-Georgetown.
Immigration Act. 1976
The Hon. Member alleged that the hold-ups in our embassies throughout the world, the bureaucratic delays, are causing some concerns. I point out to him that there are only three countries in the world which have open immigration policies today. They are Australia, the United States and Canada. Canada probably has one of the most liberal immigration programs in the world today-small "1" liberal.
The literally hundreds of thousands of applicants who wish to come into the country every year is mind-boggling. 1 have just returned from a business trip to Yugoslavia where 1 saw the line-up of people who wish to emigrate to Canada. No matter where I go in the world and no matter what embassy I visit there are line-ups of people who wish to come to Canada. Were the Hon. Member to reflect on what he said about the bureaucracy and those who work extremely hard in our embassies to try to accept applications and wade through hundreds of thousands of them, he would want to retract the accusation he made that in fact they are holding up immigration to the country. I think he will find in fact that they are not, that they are doing an excellent job under difficult circumstances in most instances and he would want to back off from that type of statement.
I will be very brief with my final point. Members of Parliament always end up dealing with the problem cases. We never hear about the cases that go through without any hitches and they are by far the majority. We hear about the problem cases and we can stand here day after day talking about them. 1 think kudos should go to the Department and to those who are involved in the immigration end of things for the great job they are doing for this country.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very attentively to the Hon. Member across the way. Perhaps if he had listened a little more attentively to what I said he would have been able to understand it. Let me repeat it a little slower so that perhaps he will be able to understand.
1 indicated very clearly to the Hon. Member that the delays that were being caused outside this country were the same as the delays we had internally with the appeals process, and that we have to deal with the number of people who can process the applicants. Very clearly, we cannot merely rubber stamp applications. We do not want undesirable people to enter this country. What we must do is increase the number of people who can deal with the process and make decisions. Leaving at the same level the number of people working in offices elsewhere in the world will not solve the problem of my constituent who waited for years and is still waiting today as we are talking to have her husband re-enter the country-

-even though they have been married for a long time. The individual in question did not enter this country illegally. He came to this country, stayed here as a student and later on got married and stayed here for some time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Why was he deported?

Immigration Act, 1976

Under the laws that exist now, the individual would be allowed to stay in the country because he had been married for a certain length of time. That law was changed only a few weeks after the individual had been deported. The law was changed by the present Minister. Before accusing my constituent, the Hon. Member should be a little more aware of the facts.
The Hon. Member said that we only hear about problem cases. I would hope so. It is our job as Member of Parliament to fix the problems of our constituents and to make this place a better place for them. It is not our job to take things that are right and make them wrong. It is our job to take things that are wrong and make them right. That is why I was elected as a Member of this House.
Finally, 1 would like to thank the Hon. Member for complimenting the previous Liberal administration on the immigration policy that was established in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: The inexperience of the Hon. Member is showing through again. The present Immigration Act was the result of the work of three Parties over a number of years. The Bill was put together by all three Parties and agreed to unanimously by all three Parties in the 1970s and was brought into effect in 1978. For him to take credit for his Party is not being entirely honest with the electorate.

Mr. Speaker, again I suppose I did not say it slowly enough. I want to thank the Hon. Member for complimenting the previous Liberal administration which was in power in 1978 at the time the law was passed. I thank him very much for that compliment to the Liberals, and a great administration it was.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in listening to the introductory remarks by the Parliamentary Secretary during his speech at third reading stage of this Bill. He referred to his constituency as being a highly ethnic one. My constituency of Winnipeg North is and has always been, since people began to move to western Canada, the gateway for immigrants to Canada, particularly for those who are usually called ethnic immigrants.
My father came to this country 80 years ago from the Ukraine. Today a very substantial number of my constituents are of Ukrainian, Polish, Jewish and German origin. We have always been proud of that. In recent years, these people have been joined by other immigrants who have come from many other countries. I know that in listing them I will miss some groups, but they have come from Portugal, China, India, the Phillippines, the West Indies, Laos, Vietnam, Chile and Yugoslavia. They have come to this country to live in my constituency, as well as in many other urban constituencies, and they are making important, useful contributions to this country.
As I am sure is the case with the Parliamentary Secretary, constituents from many of these countries regularly come to my office because they need help. What is the help they need? They need help because they have relatives they want to have join them in Canada. Very frequently these requests are
turned down. Why is this? The Government of Canada requires them to have a certain level of income so that when their relatives come to the country the applicant can guarantee that the relatives will not become a charge on the state, and the incomes of many of these people are too low. I will deal with that in a few moments. As well, they are turned down because of the kinds of jobs these prospective immigrants fulfil in Canada.
I have taken up many such cases, and I am sure in some cities like Toronto, Vancouver or Montreal in which there are many more immigrants than there are in Winnipeg, Hon. Members have taken up even more cases. I have taken such cases up with the present Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. McLean) and the present Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). Under the Liberal administration, I took up many such cases with Liberal Ministers. Time and time again I was turned down. I have frequently pleaded for the Government, Liberal or Conservative, to take a more humane attitude toward this situation. In theory, members of all Parties support family reunification. 1 thought things were going to be better with this Government.
The present Minister of State for Immigration made a statement on October 31, 1985, on this matter. This statement is reported at page 8218 of Hansard under the title "Immigration", "Future Levels of Immigration-Statement of Minister of State (Immigration)." Let me put on the record some of the things he said:
Immigration levels are being increased to 105,000 to 115,000 in 1986 and 115,000 to 125,000 in 1987 . .. During this period, the level will be rebuilt in a moderate, controlled manner which will, in a balanced way, support the reunion of families, the admission of humanitarian immigrants and the selection of economic immigrants.
He went on to say:
First, family class. The family class will remain the cornerstone of immigration policy, and we will continue to process applications on demand.
He went on:
The Government is going to emphasize increasing the number of assisted relatives and other independent applicants who have, since May 1982, been unable to emigrate without a validated job.
These individuals will be admitted on the basis of a revised selection system. Qualifications and skills will be stressed. Preference will be given, however, to assisted relatives through the allocation of bonus points.
That sounded very good, Mr. Speaker. On the same day, in commenting on that statement, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) indicated that he had certain reservations. Let me put on the record a couple of the reservations about which he spoke. In his speech he said:
The category of families and the category of assisted relatives are being unnecessarily held back by the practices of the Employment and Immigration Commission. They are being held back in three ways. One is that excessively high incomes are demanded of Canadians who wish to bring over, to sponsor an assisted relative.
Then he went on to say:
There is also the matter of the visa offices which are very poorly distributed in the countries from which many of our immigrants come, and it takes sometimes years to process an application because there is one office for India, two offices
February 25, 1986

for all of Africa, two offices for all of Central America, and those have to go through Trinidad.
Then, in referring to the Minister, he went on to say:
He has implied that there might be an increase-he has not stated it-in the family class. In fact, there is no increase.
That was last October. I have to say to the Parliamentary Secretary, as I would say to the Minister if he were here, that I find 1 am still having the same difficulties. 1 had a case from India where the application was turned down. When I pressed the Department, I received a letter giving the detailed reasons for the application being turned down. I gave it to the persons who approached me. They accepted the objections. They went back and took care of every objection; they met all the objections which were listed in the letter. Months have gone by and the applicant has still not been permitted to come to Canada.
I should like to deal with the question of income requirements. The Government says that it believes in family reunification, but if one of my constituents-and this is not only happening in the City of Winnipeg-wants to bring in his or her sister who is married and has a couple of children, the applicant is turned down because he or she does not have an income of over $20,000 per year. Not many new immigrants are so well established that they have an income of over $20,000 per year.
I could show the Minister the correspondence in one particular case. The applicant in question said: "Well, my income is a couple of thousand dollars below what you say is required. My brother is also prepared to join in the application, and our joint income is substantially higher than what is required". However, they were told that the Department does not accept joint applications and joint incomes. What the Minister implied in his statement about family reunification is not working, because the income requirements are far too high for most new immigrants.
Let me deal with another requirement. The Minister said there was a list of occupations and that if the person for whom an application was being made had those qualifications, he or she would be given points. I have the list in front of me. I say to the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary that it would be ludicrous if it were not so sad.
Let me put on the record some of the occupations which supposedly help applicants-managers in natural sciences, engineering and mathematics; managers in social sciences; administrators in medicine and health; chemists, physicists and meteorologists; civil engineers, electrical engineers and industrial engineers; economists, sociologists, social scientists and psychologists. That is just a small portion of the whole list. I ask the Parliamentary Secretary, when we talk about the kinds of people who approach me or his office, how many of them are from those groups? Very few, very few. I have looked through the list and 1 have only found two or three categories under which the kinds of people who come to me would have relatives who could qualify. If I look at the service occupations, I see specialied chefs and cooks, watch and clock repairmen, perhaps printing press occupations, and that is about it.
Immigration Act, 1976
The Minister tried to create the impression-and I assume he believed what he was saying-that because of the new approach of the Government there would be a substantial increase in the number of application for family reunification which would be approved. I say to the Minister that it will just not happen. I appeal to him and to the Government to adopt a much more humane approach to the whole question of family reunification in the immigration policy.
I will not deal with the problems of refugees. My colleague from Thunder Bay dealt with them very well. As he pointed out, the Bill is one small step, to implement one small recommendation of the many excellent recommendations made by the parliamentary committee which held a large number of meetings, and by Rabbi Plaut in his report. I hope the Government will deal with those recommendations in a humane and generous way. In my view, this Bill will do very little.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member did not want to mislead the House when he read off the list of occupations. I am familiar with the communications which he has. I point out to him, and I think he would agree, that that list opened up the Immigration Act and the approach of immigration because it allowed more independent applications to come forward. It was not through family reunification. He tied it to family reunification, which is still in existence and is working very well. It really concerns independent applications, and I wonder if the Hon. Member wants to comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to comment on that. In so far as family reunification is concerned, if the Hon. Member is correct that the list from which I quoted has nothing to do with family reunification, we are back to the situation where the person for whom the application is being made has to have a job offer in Canada which cannot be filled by a Canadian. That was the policy until very recently. Given the fact that a million and a quarter are unemployed, that virtually excludes everyone.
The Hon. Member is correct that it is for independent applicants. My fear is that the Government wants mainly to encourage-and I do not say exclusively-people to come to this country who have the money or the means to establish themselves as independent business people. While 1 am not opposed to those kinds of people coming, if it is the only thing we want to do, it is wrong and certainly mitigates against family reunification in which I am a great believer.

Mr. Speaker, 1 just want to clarify something. The Member is misleading, albeit inadvertently I am sure, the House. The point system that was allocated in the list to which he referred only enhances the opportunity for individuals to emigrate to Canada. It does not require a certified job offer. It only enhances the position of the immigrant by giving him five or ten points to add to his independent application. This tended to open up the door in some of those occupations. It is not tied to the amount of money individuals have to allow them to come here as the Member indicated. Surely he wants to set the

February 25, 1986
Immigration Act, 1976
record straight rather than leave the impression which he has left.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe that the Member listened to the remarks I made. I made two points. The first was that until very recently in order for an application to be approved the applicant had to have an offer of employment for a job which the employer and the Department of Employment and Immigration could not find a Canadian to fill. I made the point that there are very few jobs like that given the large number of unemployed. If that was changed recently, I have not heard about it and would like to know about it.
The second thing I said was that most of the people who come to my office who have applied for permission for relatives to come to join them in Canada indicate that those relatives do not have the specialized skills for 90 per cent or more of the occupations listed in this document. That is all I said. If the Member thinks I am wrong, I would be very happy to have him show me how I am wrong.

Mr. Speaker, I was listening to the Hon. Member's comments with respect to the certified job offer requirement and the new regulations which have been issued by the Department of Employment and Immigration with respect to the employment situation. I thought the Hon. Member would be aware, as I believe all other Members of the House are, that in 1982 the Government imposed the requirement of a certified job offer on independent applications for immigration to the country. That requirement meant that virtually no one could come to Canada because it was impossible to find a job which the Canada Employment Centres would certify there was no one in the country to fill.
However, as of January 1 of this year changes were made. Those changes included the list of occupations which the Hon. Member has in front of him, for which there is no longer the requirement of a certified job offer. A person who fits into those categories can now apply without having a certified job offer in the country and can come to the country under the point system as indicated by the Hon. Member.
Whether or not the people who come into his office fit into the job categories which do not require a certified job offer is another question. Since the beginning of January literally dozens of families have come to my office who wanted to bring relatives here but could not under the strict requirements of the family reunification provisions and who now see some light at the end of the tunnel. They see that there are these job categories for which there is not the requirement of a certified job offer into which their relatives and friends can fit. I am certainly finding that this is very beneficial and helpful to the people in my constituency. I am sure that if the Hon. Member takes a closer look at those categories and discusses them with the people coming into his office, he will find them most helpful to them, too.

Mr. Speaker, as I tried to make clear in my speech, it is obvious that most of the occupations on the list
really help only a very small percentage of the potential applicants. Many organizations interested in third world countries have indicated that when we make these kinds of arrangements we encourage the movement of the skilled and best educated people from those countries to Canada. Those countries need those people much more than we do in Canada. However, that is a problem which we can discuss on another occasion.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on Bill C-55. A number of speakers before me touched on a number of broad and important areas relating to immigration. There is no disagreement that the entire process of immigration is integral to what this country is about, given that to a significant extent this country is the result of individuals and families coming to the shores of Canada and building a home here. They have given to the country and, reciprocally, the country has given them a chance. Therefore, immigration is not a one-way street. The country does not only give, but receives. Immigrants who have come to the country have perhaps come with very little from an economic point of view, but with wealth and riches in social and cultural attributes.
Part of the success of our past immigration policies, and part of the respect that which Canada enjoys from nations abroad, has been based on a policy that has drawn its strength and spirit from a thrust of compassion. I hope the Government will see fit to continue a policy of immigration which is compassionate and sensitive and which speaks, not only to the domestic and narrow views and challenges which the country faces, but also to the often very difficult forces at play throughout the world. Canada must continue in future years to play the part which it has played in the past.
A number of speakers have indicated that there is a comme ci comme (a feeling with regard to Bill C-55. There are certain parts of the Bill which are good. For instance, the amendment to allow permanent residents to make appeals to the Immigration Appeal Board is a positive move. The central thrust of this legislation permits the increase of commissioners on the Immigration Appeal Board from 18 to 50. That is the main amendment to the Immigration Act which the Government is making through the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). Quite frankly, one has to say that this Bill addresses the symptom rather than the illness. It takes the easy way when immigrants and refugees are looking for concrete action.

Another part of the backlog has to do with the family reunification process. We know that generally the process is working quite well and that the vast majority of applications under the program are approved quite rapidly. The problem lies with those families who are not permitted to sponsor brothers, nephews, aunts or uncles. This is a problem to which we ought to pay closer attention. We underestimate the importance that family sponsorship can have in making a potential immigrant a successful Canadian citizen. We are undere-
February 25, 1986

stimating the resources available to an individual who has family in this country. We should be giving greater weight to applications under that program because, if we do, we would eliminate the bottle-neck that this legislation seeks to address. As 1 said, rather than addressing the cause, it prefers to address the symptoms.
The refugees affected by this bottle-neck in the system have been patient for a long time and now they are coming to Ottawa to make their case. I have met these people in my riding, as well as in cities like Montreal and Vancouver. They have been waiting for some real action. Of course, it can be argued that if we have 50 commissioners instead of 18, we will hear more applications and solve more problems. However, if we approach the problem that way, how long will it take to deal with the current backlog, not to mention the growing number of new applications each day? It will take a long, long time. Yet people are asking for something to speed up the process, as well as make it more compassionate and more fair and understanding. We do not want an adversarial situation involving the applicant and the Immigration Appeal Board.
I have had instances in my own riding where people have to come before the IAB with solicitors to prove their case to the ultimate degree. There is a family in my riding which has been in this country for three years. Before the establishment of the new civilian Government in Argentina they had to escape the military regime because they were both professors at universities in Buenos Aires. One of the first groups to be persecuted by the Argentine military regime was the Academe. They left their country with their children and tried to establish a new life in this country. Now, after more than three years in Canada, after establishing themselves here, after acquiring English as a second language at night school, after holding down menial jobs because their degrees were not recognized here, which is another significant problem we have overlooked, and after their children have been Canadianized and now speak English rather than Spanish, they are being asked to return to Argentina because it is deemed to be safe under a civilian government.
That might be true to a certain degree. For the moment things are a little more tranquil and secure under a civilian government. However, how can we know what will happen tomorrow?
This family is afraid to go back to their home country because they fear persecution in the future. They fear for the future of their children in that country. They would rather stay in Canada. They are contributing members of this society. They both work, pay their taxes and contribute to the social and economic wealth of this country. Therefore, should we not stop and think about whether we ought to send them back, having made them go through the IAB process to state their case time after time after time?
What do we mean when we talk about compassion in Canada? What do we mean when we say we should address the cause of a problem rather than the symptoms? We mean that we should not take the narrow-minded approach which says let us increase the number of immigration officers and, if
Immigration Act, 1976
that does not work, introduce another Bill and increase the number again. No, there comes a time when you must look at the problem and say enough is enough. We cannot allow ourselves to introduce bank-aid solutions because they will not work. It might be a good public relations gimmick, but deep in our hearts we know it is not the proper way to address the depth of a serious and growing problem.
The Minister also talked about fighting to eradicate phoney refugee applicants. He is right to a certain degree because there are individuals who take advantage of the system to the detriment of those who have a legitimate case. Therefore, the Minister is in part correct to ask his officials to try and weed out those applicants who make life difficult for the majority of people with legitimate cases. However, the Minister failed to go after the growing industry involving phoney immigration consultants and lawyers. I am getting sick and tired of talking to constituents and sponsors of immigrants, as well as to refugee applicants, who have paid hundreds if not thousands of dollars to these low-lifes who do nothing to aid their case. Individual lawyers and consultants simply use that as a scam to make a dollar. Individuals are using these people to pay for the shingle they have outside their office. It is growing and becoming more serious.
I had a case in Toronto last week of a Portuguese individual who was just there visiting for three months. No one knew that he was coming for a visit, in terms of the bureaucracy. He got a call from a so-called immigration consultant asking him if he required his services to stay in the country. When the visitor suggested that he was only here on a visit the so-called consultant said, "Yeah, that's for sure. I have heard that before". Therefore, that also speaks to a wheel in the system that is connecting these phoney consultants to potential cases for them.
If we are prepared to rid the system of phoney refugees in this country then we also have to apply equal force to those people in this society who live off the proceeds of immigrants who do not know any better and place their trust in these individuals. The immigrant may not speak the language very well and, therefore, they are very much impressed by the pinstriped blue suit and tie individual who comes and says, "A thousand dollars and I will get your cousin into this country". These are not isolated cases because I have heard about them from other colleagues in the House as well. Therefore 1 urge the Minister and this Government to have the compassion and the courage to stamp out what I would suggest is a very serious white-collar crime.
When we also talk about being compassionate and being progressive, which our immigration policies have been, we must also recognize those individuals who come to this country with degrees and professions. Quite often what happens when they come into this country is that the degrees are not recognized. After years of training in their own reputable universities and educational institutions in their home countries they come to this country and take jobs as janitors, construction

February 25, 1986
Immigration Act, 1976
aides and the like. I am not suggesting that those occupations are demeaning, by any means I am suggesting that when an individual who has taught in his home country and cannot get a teaching profession here and is forced to clean and scrub floors when, in fact, that individual could be contributing in a different sense, then that too is incorrect and needs addressing.
There was a disagreement in terms of individuals that were allowed into this country perhaps because they had more money. I believe the Member from Winnipeg was alluding to that. 1 think perhaps what he was alluding to was the whole question of entrepreneurial immigrants. Last year the Standing Committee on Employment, Labour and Immigration, which obviously has a majority of Conservative Members, was dangerously toying with concepts of entrepreneurial immigration.
Let me point out very quickly at the beginning of this debate that I support a stream of entrepreneurial immigration. In fact, it was the Liberal Party which was in Government that sponsored and introduced such a stream, but we never intended to make it a cornerstone, or to elevate the whole entrepreneurial stream to the detriment of others. The Immigration Committee was toying very dangerously with boosting up the entrepreneurial element to a degree that was overriding the others. It is a mistake, because while we require entrepreneurs, foreign investment, individuals who are willing to invest and start to build companies and enterprises in this country, we also have to realize the history of this country. We must take into consideration the plight of other individuals who, while they are not wealthy and do not bring extraordinary amounts of money into this country, bring something else that this country depended on years ago. I would submit to you that this country will require that reinforcement in the years to come.
Many poor immigrants have joined Canada's entrepreneurs, and some have joined Canada's wealthy circle. Many immigrants have brought trades to this country and have taken jobs that you and I perhaps do not want to do. They work from seven in the morning until seven at night, often six days a week. I am not suggesting that those jobs are demeaning. All I am suggesting is that there are those individuals across the globe who are prepared to come to this country to enjoy the opportunities here and undertake those types of positions, and we have to be sensitive their situations.
When we talk about occupations I think there tends to be conflicting information. I have contractors in Toronto in my constituency who say that, "We cannot find enough certified and qualified bricklayers", for instance, or "carpenters, plumbers, electricians, tool and dye makers". Yet when I have individuals who are sponsoring relatives from abroad who happen to be carpenters or plumbers what they are told is that we have an abundance of those individuals in Canada, many of whom are unemployed. So there tends to be a conflicting nature which really needs to be updated. We really need to be with the times. Do we need to fill those types of positions or do we not? I am running into a lot of conflicting evidence that says the contrary.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. McDermid) said, "We only get the problematic cases". We sometimes get the more problematic cases, but I would also submit to him that we also get the average run-of-the-mill cases, individuals who come to the Member of Parliament first rather than going down to Bloor Street and visiting their immigration officer. So we get a lot of standard, average, every day applications. We need to pay attention to those problems and difficulties; not only the problematic ones, but those that are reflective of the pool of applications that the bureaucratics are facing. I am not suggesting, and neither is this Party, that the bureaucrats go out of their way to take their sweet time in processing applications.
There are places in this world such as Hong Kong and New Delhi where it takes three years to process an application. I would submit to him that that is not good enough, and that rather than placing blame we should be trying to address the cause and not the symptom.
I realize you are motioning that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. 1 would once again like to appeal to this House to be somewhat more compassionate, somewhat more courageous, and use a little conviction when we are speaking of immigration, rather than trying to touch the superficial element in dealing with the symptoms rather than the cure. Let's address, attack and whip the cause of the difficulties. Let's make Canada a country that is a lot more just.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, when this Bill was introduced in the House last June the Minister said that his principal purpose was to deal with the refugee backlog, which at that time was around 15 or 16,000 persons. It was rather strange that the Minister should put forward this Bill to deal with the refugee backlog, because the Minister had received in April of 1985, just a few months previous, the Plaut Report which dealt with the refugee determination process on a broad basis and made many recommendations to deal with that entire problem. We now know that in Canada over the last few years there has been a great increase in refugees from many troubled spots in the world. I guess that is a symptom of the political disruptions which are taking place on many continents. There are refugees from Central America, Africa, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Indochina and Central and Eastern Europe. There has been a great increase in the number of refugees coming to Canada claiming refugee status. Therefore, there has been an increasing backlog which led to the Minister, under the previous Government, appointing both the Ratushny and Plaut commissions to study this matter.
The Plaut Commission reported several recommendations to the present Minister in April, 1985. However, in June we saw Bill C-55 which attempts to deal with the problem simply by increasing the number of people on the Immigration Appeal Board to 50 members. That has been criticized as a solution because it is simply a band-aid solution to deal with symptoms and does not really deal with the causes of the problem.
February 25, 1986

Furthermore, it is a complete disregard of the recommendations made by the Plaut commission.
What did the Government do? In its usual way it introduced the Bill in June, 1985, but also made a reference to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration to study the Plaut report and the whole process of refugee determination. Eventually the same committee was referred Bill C-55. Therefore, the committee had before it at the same time, Bill C-55 dealing with this increase in membership on the Immigration Appeal Board as well as the reference to study the Plaut commission recommendations and the refugee determination process.
The Bill has been returned to the House with one minor amendment from committee. We also have two reports presented by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration dealing with the process of refugee determination and the refugee claimant backlog. I believe that they are good reports and have the unanimous support in principle of all the Parties in the House.
The committee, made up of Conservative, Liberal and New Democratic members, put forward several recommendations to deal with the entire problem of refugee determination in this country and the backlog which now amounts to some 19,000 applicants. One must remember that the process was complicated still further following the Supreme Court decision in the Singh case on April 4, 1985. The decision was that by virtue of our new Charter of Rights, all applicants for refugee status had a right to an oral hearing before the Immigration Appeal Board. That meant the process was made more complex and more time consuming.
The Standing Committee dealt with that and made recommendations. Although their report was tabled in the late fall, we still do not have a Bill from the Government to implement the recommendations put forward by that committee.
We set out certain principles in that report to which we all agreed. We said that four basic principles are fundamental to the approach of the Standing Committee and the recommendations it has made. Consequently we recommend first, that it is the committee's strongly held conviction that Canadians do not want people sent back to countries where they have been persecuted or where they still may be persecuted because it conflicts with our basic principles of justice and fair play. People should be treated in a humane fashion and should not be sent back to countries where they will be executed for political reasons.
Second, we said that every person in Canada who wishes to claim that he or she is a Convention refugee should have an unqualified right of access to a formal process that will adjudicate the claim.
Third, all Convention refugee claimants should have their case decided at a non-adversarial oral hearing. In this respect we were following the decision in the Singh case before the Supreme Court.
Fourth, we said that the decision maker in the formal process, whatever that process should be, shall have the power
Immigration Act, 1976
in addition to declaring an individual to be a Convention refugee, to recommend to the Minister that specific individuals who are not within the strict definition of Convention refugee nevertheless be considered for landing on compassionate and humanitarian grounds.
The committee studied this in some depth and heard from many witnesses, both with respect to Bill C-55 and the Plaut report and refugee determination. The committee's recommendations are substantial, well founded and the result of much consultation. On the other hand, this Bill is not the result of much consultation and is simply a confused half measure to deal with a serious problem. It contains a few clauses that are good policy and an improvement to the Immigration Act, but they are a minor part of the Bill.
The over-all solution in this Bill is not what is needed, nor what the witnesses recommended. It is not what Plaut recommended.
We agree that by appointing more people to the Immigration Appeal Board the process will be expedited. However, if that is all that is done, it is an unfair and outdated process that is being expedited without getting to the bottom of the problems confronting refugees who have been waiting a long time-several years for some-to have their case heard by the Immigration Appeal Board. The Bill does not deal with the problems studied by Plaut and the committee.
While we are unhappy with the Bill, there are certain merits to it. However, we want the Government to introduce a Bill which will implement the recommendations put forward in the fifth and sixth reports of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration that were presented by its chairman, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). I believe they are excellent reports and, if implemented by legislation, will meet the needs of refugees in this country. I wish the Parliamentary Secretary or the Minister would intervene in this debate to tell us when that legislation implementing those two reports will be introduced. Such legislation, combined with the provisions of this Bill, would make sense, but this Bill alone is a half-way measure and cannot be supported with very great enthusiasm by Members of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a poll published recently by the Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses revealed that the rate at which small and medium-sized businesses in Canada are closing has dropped to its lowest level in sixteen years.

subtopic: CALL FOR CLOSURE OF TAX LOOPHOLE
CALL FOR CLOSURE OF TAX LOOPHOLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) prepares to bring down the Budget tomorrow, 1 again want to appeal to him to put an end to the abuse of limited partnership provisions in the Income Tax Act, provisions which have become the biggest, costliest, and most wasteful tax loophole since the scientific research tax credit.
As the chairperson of the Tax Probe 86 Committee, I recently became aware of the following example. A company in Manitoba called Organic Research Limited advertised to potential investors that for $50,000 they could reap the following benefits: a $10,000 reduction in taxes from the investment tax credit, a $20,000 tax saving through the flow-through share provisions, and the company would buy back the shares for $29,000 almost immediately. This adds up to nearly $60,000 in benefits for an investment of $50,000, courtesy of the taxpayers of Canada.
This is even more ludicrous when one considers that Organic Research Limited is doing research into turning trees into sugar, at a time when the sugar-beet industry in southern Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba is on its knees. It is time that this nonsense was stopped.

I wish to illustrate my point by outlining a case involving a man who came to see me. I will not give his name. However, I will say that he is a sawmill worker in British Columbia. He came to Canada from India in 1970. He has worked in a sawmill since 1971 as a sawyer. He is a good worker and makes about $14.86 per hour. He has been steadily employed since he came to Canada. It is a tough job in the mills and he performs it well.
He became a Canadian citizen in 1974. He married in 1982. As is the Indian custom, he married a woman in India. On June 15, 1983, he applied to have his wife come to join him in Canada. There was a delay with respect to his application. He contacted the Department of Immigration and there was a further delay. His application was ultimately refused. He filed an appeal on September 25, 1985. There will now be another delay. He was told that the delay will be at least 18 months before his appeal can be heard.
In cases such as this I have often found that the appeals are won. The appeal tribunal will often rule that, for instance in this case, it is a valid marriage and the appeal will be allowed. What will happen then is that he will have to apply again and there will be another delay of about one year.
Here we have a case of a man who was married in 1983. His appeal may be heard in 1987 and by 1988 he should be able to have his wife come to Canada. That is five years during which he has had to live apart from his wife. I say that is cruel. I do not think that is a good system of justice at all.
As well, there is an additional problem in this case. As is often the case, this man will not be able to have his wife come to visit in this five-year time span because when she goes to apply for a visitor's visa immigration officials will say that they had better not let her come to Canada because what she may do is stay here. She would then have to be deported and that would be a messy procedure. Immigration officials do not trust people in these situations to visit Canada because, after all, they have already applied to get into the country and are not really regular visitors. The man in my case is caught in a Catch-22 situation. He has to wait for the appeal process and cannot bring his wife to Canada as a visitor. What kind of way is that to treat a Canadian citizen? In this case, I think I will mention the name of the person involved. The man's name is Mr. Major Dwaliwal. I am sure he would want me to do this, in the sense that his case is typical of many cases which come before the Department of Immigration.

While I have a chance I would like to make the point that this is a problem of delay for this man. I think it is a matter of a cruel delay. There is a secondary problem resulting from it in that he cannot even have his wife come to visit him in Canada.
1 do not think that is a correct procedure.
While I am on my feet with respect to the immigration matter, I wish to draw to the Minister's attention another series of cases which were brought to my attention through my constituency office in Vancouver. A few Saturdays ago I was visited by a group of doctors. These were medical doctors from different countries. All of them are citizens of Canada or landed immigrants. Several of the doctors had been asked to come to Canada with the possibility of practising medicine in Canada being held out to them. It was pointed out to them that they could contribute something to the country and that they could gain as well. There were 12 doctors in this group. All of them had degrees and credentials recognized by the World Health Organization and by the Medical Council of Canada based here in Ottawa.
In order to intern in Canada two requirements must be met. First, one has to pass an exam in Canada and be evaluated by the Medical Council of Canada. Second, after the exam, one must find an intern position, after which time one becomes a doctor. The problem we have is that this is a group of foreign doctors who have become Canadian citizens. They have emigrated to Canada and cannot obtain intern positions here.
I promised this group that I would bring this situation to the attention of the Minister. It is an important problem and a very serious one for these people. I know because I met with them personally. They are good people, well-educated and willing to contribute here in Canada. As a matter of fact, they told me that there was not an over-supply of doctors in certain areas of Canada and that they would be prepared to go to these outlying areas if only they could intern in Canada. They told me that certain areas of Canada are not being served by local graduates and that they were willing to serve in these areas for three years, for example, after interning in Canada. However, the obstacle before them is that they cannot get internship positions.
When I spoke to these people I found that there was a pattern of discrimination here. Graduates of Canadian medical schools are getting internships. However, these people are not, and I have to make the point again that they are Canadian citizens. They are different in the sense that they were educated abroad, but their credentials are recognized after passing an appropriate test in Canada. They are qualified and they are Canadian citizens but they cannot get internships.
Remember, Mr. Speaker, that these are Canadian citizens who were educated in foreign medical schools, so I will call them foreign medical graduates. Apparently, 500 foreign medical graduates applied for internships and about 23 received them. That is a pretty low ratio. They told me that medical examinations are conducted in 23 different countries and those who take the examinations are given false hopes
