about what will happen when they get to Canada. They give up their jobs and come to Canada to become doctors in Canada.
Why are these examinations given if they mean nothing? Why is there a gap between what the Government of Canada says and what the medical profession in Canada does? It seems that the medical profession is more powerful than the Government.
It appears that there is a pattern of discrimination on the part of the Canadian medical profession which prefers to take local graduates as interns rather than foreign graduates. I would go so far as to say that this pattern of discrimination is in fact illegal.
On talking to these foreign medical graduates I found that they were in desperate situations. I talked to one man who could not even get a technician's job. When he applied for such a job, he was told that he could not have it because he is a doctor. He said that he was not a doctor because he could not get an internship, but they said they could not hire him because he was a doctor. He is in a never-never land. He is a doctor but he is not a doctor.
One man to whom I spoke applied as a nursing orderly. Can you believe it, Mr. Speaker? He is a foreign medical graduate who came to Canada, passed a Canadian exam, could not get accepted as an intern, applied as a nursing orderly and could not even get that job.
Two provinces in Canada seem to have avoided this situation, Manitoba and Quebec. These provinces have made an effort to offer equality of positions to foreign medical graduates.
I take the opportunity of this debate to draw this particular problem to the attention of the House of Commons, the Canadian people, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), who I see in the House, and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). I would like to conclude by reading into the record a letter sent to me by Dr. Kanwarjit Singh on behalf of the Committee of Graduates of Foreign Medical Schools. After passing the Medical Council of Canada Evaluating Examination, we are theoretically eligible for postgraduate training on the same basis as any Canadian medical graduate. From this point on there should be no distinction between medical graduates from Canadian and non-Canadian medical schools. However, in practice it doesn't work this way.

Mr. Speaker, I am wondering if the Hon. Member could tell us of some of his own personal experiences in the City of Vancouver with respect to the delays that are currently being experienced by those who are waiting to appear before the Immigration Appeal Board, and tell us whether or not he feels that the increase in the numbers of representatives, paltry though it be, will have any impact on that.

Mr. Speaker, there are delays and it is one of the biggest problems with immigration. We have to balance two things. We have to speed up the rate at which the cases are heard, but in doing this we also have to make sure that there is a just system. In this case, that system is probably an adversarial system where justice can be rendered. We do want to speed up the hearing of the appeals but we do not want to lose the justice and due process. This is a balancing act the Government has to consider.
I personally am in favour of creating more positions as long as they will be staffed by good people and not simply be excuses for patronage like the Liberals used in previous incarnations.
That's what I get for handing him a lob.

No, there are some very good people on the Immigration Appeal Boards as well. 1 think we have to speed up the process a bit but we have to balance it with the need for having a just hearing. Yes, the answer is that there are many cases out there, and that is one of the big problems in immigration.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that Bill C-55 deals with a very specific element of our immigration policy, the appointment of the number of people who will be in positions to oversee the tremendous backlog of applications for refugee status. However, it seems that the opportunity given us by third reading of the Bill is to examine some of the questions which were not put before the House in Bill form, and to examine some of the questions which have been ignored to date on a systemic basis.
There has certainly been a crying need over the last number of years for a total review of immigration policy, not only with the view of encouraging more people to come to this great country, but of determining that support systems are available for those people whom we welcome into our country either as refugees of a political nature or under the family reunification program.
I should like to deal, first and foremost, with the issue of family reunification. Most of us in our capacity as Members of Parliament-and it is certainly the case in the riding of Hamilton East-represent people of many different cultures and from many different countries. 1 face a demand as a Member of Parliament from families who have tried every means of facilitating reunification with their loved ones in other countries. There are times in my office on a Saturday morning when I will have a family in tears. In fact, about a week ago I was most pleased to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) say that he was working very hard to facilitate the reunification of the Estonian family, a situation which was raised by a Member from the City of Toronto. That two-year old child, about whom the Minister spoke, is not alone in being isolated from her family.
There was a couple in my office last week who were forced to leave their eight-year old daughter in Romania. They applied for a visa and had to wait a very long time for it. When the visa was accorded, the Government would not allow the child to leave with the parents and she stayed in the care of the grandparents. The parents have been in Canada since September of 1984, and have applied for political refugee status. They have been waiting for their case to be heard. Their case is clear, they are legitimate political refugees. In the meantime, their daughter languishes in Romania. She has been punished by the Romanian Government to the extent that she is not allowed to go to school. This eight-year old child has been separated from her parents for almost 19 months and has been punished to the point of being denied an education.
While it is admirable of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to raise issues of individual concern, he must recognize that this is not an isolated case. The situation faced by the Estonian family is faced by hundreds and thousands of families across Canada. People are going to bed every night with their hearts breaking. There was a woman crying in my office just last week because she longed for her daughter. She did not know whether she would see her daughter again or when the Canadian Government was going to deal with her application.

They have not been denied by the Canadian Government, but are on the list of the 20,000 people who are waiting for a fair hearing, which is the right of immigrants to Canada.
We have heard the other side of the story, Mr. Speaker. One of the things that politicians must face in Canadian society is a certain level of bigotry, of fear, and of racism directed toward the people who would, allegedly, steal our jobs. 1 have heard it in my own riding. People call me up and ask why I am fighting on behalf of immigrants who came to this country and stole our jobs. However, we know full well that immigration creates jobs. People who are working, in many cases for a minimum wage, and are pooling their resources, are forced to spend almost every last penny of their earnings to keep themselves afloat. These people are contributing to the economy in a far more direct way than those of us who can afford to sock away our dollars or benefit from a capital gains exemption. Every dollar paid in a salary to immigrants is spent because those immigrants want to establish themselves. They want to buy a home.
I had a very personal experience in the days of the exodus of refugees from Vietnam. 1 was involved with a group that sponsored a family from Vietnam. At that time I took over publicity for Operation Lifeline. I received hate letters and calls from people asking why I was getting involved with these people. The members of the family that I helped to sponsor are now working, although not at great jobs. One of them eventually got a job at a major steel mill and then was laid off, like many other people. However, most of them are working at jobs in clothing factories where they are earning only a little more than minimum wage. A couple of them are working in restaurants.
It is wonderful to see what they have done and to see the joy on their son's face because he is taking piano lessons. He is a great musician. Mr. Speaker, I realize that that family has taken nothing from the country; in fact, it has given. That family has shown what a family can do when it puts its hearts and minds together and is prepared to live in crowded circumstances and to pool its resources.
Public policy of immigration should be used to facilitate that kind of reunification and to facilitate the immigration of people to this country who stand a good chance of making it and of making an economic contribution. I was disappointed last year when the Committee on Immigration took the position that we should be considering increases in the area of entrepreneurship. It is not that I am against entrepreneurs. More power to you if you can make a buck through the sweat of your brow and your own imagination. However, I also think that the so-called entrepreneur program, which basically defines someone who has money, should not necessarily be the criterion upon which we encourage people to come to this country. My great uncle may have died and bequeathed me $.5 million, but does that mean I would necessarily make a contribution to our economy? If one looks at Canadian success stories, in many cases those people came to this country as immigrants with $10, $20, or $100 in their pockets. My ancestors were driven out of their country during the potato
famine because they did not have enough to eat, and they came to Canada.
I would like to refer to what we have been doing with Bill C-55 and other legislation which considers the question of family reunification as it relates to those with disabilities. I think a lot of people are praying that the changes which were recommended in the equality report, as it deals with immigration, will be implemented.

Specifically, Mr. Speaker, there is one question that was never addressed by the Committee or by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. MacDonald), and that is the question of the immigration of young children or relatives who are less developed mentally. I am not sure about the French term, but in English the term used to be:

-mentally retarded child or developmentally retarded child, not a developmentally advanced child. 1 can give the Minister chapter and verse of cases which have been brought to my attention of people who have been denied reunification with their children because the children have been defined by a medical expert, or whatever, as not having an IQ high enough to come to this country. In some cases they are working on farms and able to support themselves in their home country, but they are denied the right to come to Canada. I am pleased that the equality report which followed the Charter is recommending to the Government that we change the discriminatory clauses in our Immigration Act which prevent people from coming to Canada if they have been classified as being in that so-called sub-group of developmentally handicapped, because that is not fair.
In the same way we should be considering the establishment of a process which will permit people from countries other than the white Anglo-Saxon countries to get a fair shake with regard to immigration. I have many friends from India as well as Pakistan who have been extremely disconcerted by the attitude which they sometimes face when, with the assistance of relatives here in Canada, they make application in their home country. In many cases they have to travel hundreds, if not thousands, of miles to arrive at the consulate only to be told that their birth certificate or their marriage certificate is invalid. Perhaps their way of doing things is not exactly the way in which we operate here in Canada. We must build in, not only flexibility, but also sensitivity.
I was pleased when, some months ago, by way of intervention from the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) and myself we were successful in convincing the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) to issue a special visa to a family that came from Iran. I hope this message reaches thoses people who are working on the front lines. Like the people who work in your constituency office, Mr. Speaker, they may have all the best intentions in the world. They are on the front lines for Canada and, even if the answer is not a positive one, at the very least they should be decent, polite, and accommodating.

This particular family had a daughter-in-law and a son living in Canada with a four-year-old child. They had five other children living in Iran and had no intention of immigrating to Canada. They wanted to come to see their son, whom they had not seen for seven years, and his new wife and their new granchild. Because of the difficult political situation in Iran, when the visa was issued they had to leave the country immediately. The visa was not issued for Canada because there is not a Canadian embassy there. They were advised to go to Switzerland and make an application at the Canadian consulate in Switzerland and they did so. When they arrived in Switzerland the immediate reaction of the official involved was that these people were from Iran. "There is no way we touch Iranians because they are coming to this country to live, they are not here on valid visitor's permits", he said. All the long-distance phone calls from my office or that of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain were not going to convince this particular official that this family was coming to Canada to see a son they had not seen in seven years and a grandchild who was then, I think, four years old.
We intervened with the Minister and she took the bull by the horns and said she would issue the permit, which she did. For that we were very grateful. Unfortunately, many people do not realize that they have that recourse, that you can get all of the Parties together even when the House is not sitting, or that the Minister's disposition is going to be as positive in other cases as it was in this.
Obviously the Minister cannot deal with every single immigration issue which crosses the desk of every official. The point is that we have an obligation to develop systems which take into consideration the needs, not only of those people who are working in the hinterlands, as it were, in our consulates and immigration offices, but we also have to build systems which will offset the kind of endemic and systemic discrimination we have seen in the backlog of refugee applications. Most of those people are not necessarily coming from what we would call the traditional white anglo-saxon countries. They come from countries where political unrest is something we only see on television and hope will never happen here. We have to develop a system which will not only take that into consideration, but one which will keep paramount the notion that family reunification should be the number one objective of our immigration policy. You can lose your money, you can lose your home and a lot of other things, but if you have your family you have something to build on. There is a built-in bonus to a policy which says that when the number of immigrants is to be increased-and I believe it should be, and substantially so. Because it creates jobs and increases economic activity, let us not do it just for those people who have $250,000 or $500,000 to invest. Frankly, most people are not in that range.
There is a lot of work to be done in this area. I have files here, and there are dozens and dozens more where they came from, concerning people who have had a problem with the system. I am afraid that a two-page Bill dealing with the single issue of more appointments to the IAB will not solve these

problems. What we need is a long-term look at where we are going, how we can open our doors, how we can encourage more immigration to help build Canada. This country was built by the work of immigrants and their families and that is the kind of policy we should be implementing as we enter the 21st century.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member spent considerable time on the lengthy process involved in getting applications started and completed. 1 wonder if she has had experience with the long and sometimes tedious process that refugees have to go through only to find themselves suspended, as it were, by the Department, sometimes for several years. Can she comment on that particular problem?

Mr. Speaker, in some cases these individuals are faced with a double whammy. They may have fled their country because of political or economic persecution, or a general lack of individual freedom. They come to Canada, make application as bona fide political refugees, yet in many cases are denied the opportunity to seek gainful employment, for example, while their application is under review. Obviously if the application takes years-and we have seen a number of refugees who have waited two or three years-they have to be either a self-supporting millionaire or have an awful lot of friends in order to survive. If they are able to work, in many cases they establish themselves as part of the community. I had a gentleman in my office a couple of weeks ago who has been working as a baker. He has been in this country for a number of years. He has a second job as a fur-cutter. This is a very specific profession. Yet, because of some of the regulations and/or delays, he is facing great financial hardship.
Obviously these questions can be addressed only through an over-all look at the problem. It cannot be done simply by attempting to deal with one particular problem involving the Immigration Appeal Board. Tripling the number of members will not solve the problem when you have a backlog of thousands. It would be unfair to suggest to the public that this Bill is the answer. Obviously it will speed up the process to the tune of a few dozen a week, but when you have thousands of people waiting, they are going to be waiting for a very long time.

I cannot understand why we are not approaching this problem in a more systematic and serious way. I just wondered if that

Mr. Speaker, 1 happen to have been lucky enough in my constituency office to have had an excellent assistant on these matters in the person of Don Drury. Unfortunately, because we cannot afford to pay our people as well as do other Government sectors, he has had to go on to greener pastures, and I am really sorry to see him go. That being said, let me point out that we seem to stick to a kind of Canadian cultural practice in this area. Too many of my Italian-Canadi-an friends, for example, if you are compare, you can be a brother-in-law, sister-in-law, aunt, or uncle, and you are all family. They do not make the distinction we do regarding the son, daughter or father type of relationship. They reach out. If you are from the same village, you are compare.
We have to look at expanding the definition so that those relatives who are now being refused are given greater consideration because they already have a support system here. In my own community, the Agro family from Racalmuto came to Canada in the late 1940s because the doors were open to them. Now there are more people from that village living in Hamilton than there are in Racalmuto. I think most of them have the last name of Agro. They would argue that they are all related, and I am sure that that is so in heart if not in bloodline, but I think the Hon. Member made a very good point.

There was one other point that I wanted to ask the Member to comment on, and that was a statement she made, which is often contradicted by general acceptance across the country, that is, that the increase of immigrants increases the economic activity of Canada, rather than the myth which is propagated most generally that immigrants take Canadians' jobs and, therefore, put Canadians out of work. I would like her to comment or to enlarge on that a little bit.

I am sure there are people here in this room today who have come from another country with very little but have been prepared to invest in this country. I have friends today who are working in sewing factories making $4.50 an hour. They might come home with a pay cheque of $160, $170, $180 a week. That money goes to buy clothing, because they have come to the country as political refugees, for example, with nothing but the clothes on their backs. That money goes to buy food. It goes to buy, in many cases, shelter and a roof over their heads. I think you see many, many immigrants who believe in the dream of home ownership and they pool their resources at an early stage to buy a home. That money may go to buy a washing machine. When you are at a lower income level, which would primarily represent the income level of most immigrants coming to this country, as soon as you get a pay cheque you take it out and spend it in the community.
If you are in the $50,000 plus income bracket many of your dollars are spent moving around T bills or investing in something which does not create direct jobs either for your community or for the country. You are playing on the stock market or you are moving your money around in that way, but that money has less of a direct feeding effect into the economy, less of an injection, less of a boost than the money of the family that comes here and makes collectively between a husband and a wife working maybe only $20,000 or $25,000. If that money is put together to get a house, to get food, to buy a car, to buy necessities in Canadian life, then that money is going right back into the economy. That is why I think that immigrants in fact create employment rather than take it away from Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I will just make a very brief intervention. I want to reiterate a number of the points that have been made this afternoon, for instance, the point made by the Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) just a moment ago when she indicated that we impose upon immigrants who come to Canada a family structure which they sometimes do not recognize. They wonder why we do not recognize that somebody coming from their country wants to bring over his or her family.
For instance, I can give you a very personal experience which I had. I lived for a number of years in Nigeria at the time that the census was taken. When the census taker came around to my house we had a Canadian girl staying with us. The census taker was in quite a quandary because, although we were in the Moslem part of the country, she was not another wife, nor was she a daughter or a sister. When he asked me if she was my sister, I said no. Finally, the census taker asked me, "Does she come from your country?". When I explained to him, "Yes, she came from a part of my country", he said, "Oh, that's fine", and he put her down as a sister, and that was very acceptable to him and to everybody. In fact, it was the only category into which she could fit.
I also want to reiterate the concern that many people have about immigration and the concern which not only the immigrants but the people in Canada feel in dealing with immigrants who have come to Canada. I am referring to the ability of the Department of suspend people somewhere between the time of their decision to apply, the final possibility that they might land or even be in Canada, and, even beyond that, when they might become citizens of Canada. I remender a couple of years ago, as members of the Public Accounts Committee, we were looking into the real delays that veterans were experiencing in getting their pensions. We were told by veterans who appeared before our committee that sometimes it took five years from the time they applied for a veteran's allowance or a veteran's pension until they went through all the processes and finally got a veteran's pension. This is within our bureaucracy. I think that in the case of immigrants we have managed to stretch far beyond that because we now have situations where immigrants wait for years and years.
I have a neighbour in my home constituency who has been a refugee for a number of years and for some reason, even after
February 25, 1986

he was designated as a refugee, he was unable to get himself designated as a landed immigrant. He has already been here five years.
When we deal with Bill C-55, which is the Act to amend the Immigration Act, we think that we are changing the process for the better, but it becomes obvious, once you start going through this structure and you delve into the problems we have regarding the people immigrating to the country, that what we are doing is applying a few band-aids which are not really going to make very much difference into the total and final effectiveness of the Act. What the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has announced to the world is that until now we have been accepting 85,000 immigrants, and a little more with the reunification of families and so on, we are telling the world now that we are going to start accepting 120,000 per year. We are increasing the number by approximately 25 per cent. However, in doing so we have not put in place the kind of processing ability which would make it possible for us to have a smooth operating machine so when these people apply they can be processed. Just imagine sitting in a community in South America, Vietnam or Hong Kong and knowing that you have put in an application, and then waiting for five years to get a reply from the local immigration officer, or even in fact never getting a reply from the local immigration officer, being ignored entirely, not necessarily by what they consider to be the local bureaucrat, but being ignored by Canada. It seems they are being ignored by Canada because we do not have the necessary facilities to allow for quick processing of these applicants.
Our treatment of applicants is not good. Rather than accepting their application they should be told that nothing can be done for them. There are cases where we advertise for immigrants yet we hinder them from immigrating to this country so that they eventually give up and decide not to come. I am surprised that we have as many immigrants as we do when one considers the persistence that is necessary to become a landed immigrant.
Those whose applications are eventually processed are thankful for their acceptance by Canadians. However, if they find they are unable to establish themselves within our structure they face numerous delays, which we would not accept as Canadians. Landed immigrants face so many road-blocks in their pursuit of landed immigrant status that many believe we do not want them to become citizens.
Furthermore, those who have obtained landed immigrants status and wish to bring their families for a visit should ensure that the latter do not apply for immigration before visiting. The bureaucrats in the Department will suggest that they cannot allow a family member to come to Canada for a visit because they have applied for landed immigrant status. No matter what assurances are made that the family member will return home, the bureaucrat assumes that that person cannot be trusted to return. The Department of Employment and
Canadian Arsenals Limited
Immigration will not allow them to enter Canada on a visitor's permit if they have applied for landed immigrant status.
When considering a Bill such as this we must take the opportunity to consider the problems that are not solved by this Bill and ensure that we have a smooth mechanism for quickly processing these other 30,000 immigrants to Canada so they do not feel rejected in this country.

Canadian Arsenals Limited

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: When the House last debated the Bill, the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) had the floor. Since he is not here, we will resume debate.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to join in debate on Bill C-87, an Act to allow the federal Government to dispose of Canadian Arsenals Limited. However, it is not because I agree with the Government's objective-just the opposite. It gives us the opportunity to explore how the Government's ideology can lead it to make such financial mistakes. It also gives us the opportunity to point out the weaknesses in the proposal before us, particularly in the way it has been carried through. Finally, we are given the opportunity to state our regret at the Government's desire to dispose of Canadian Arsenals Limited.
This corporation, which manufactures large calibre munitions, including tank ammunition, has been in existence as a Crown corporation for just over 40 years. The proposal is to sell this corporation to a Montreal engineering firm named SNC. That corporation, through its ownership of Canadian Arsenals Limited as well as IVI Incorporated, which has been operating for some time, will be allowed to become a monopolist in Canada of the manufacture of munitions for the Department of National Defence.
I believe this decision by the Government is regrettable. Canadian Arsenals Limited does 90 per cent of its business with the federal Government. We trust that it operates as efficiently as all other Crown corporations. We assume that sales are made to the Government at the lowest possible price. If excessive profits are being made, they would come back to the Government soon enough and would be available to offset costs. We have a situation, then, in which there cannot be any profiteering in the production of ammunition, yet we can be sure that the Canadian Department of National Defence will have the ammunition it needs and there will not be any of several kinds of risks being run.
The fact is that Canadian Arsenals has been quite successful as a commercial enterprise. It is on the list of Canada's 500 largest companies. It was third in a list of companies which have had the best profit record over the past five years. Admittedly, one might say it was a very difficult five years with the interest rate depression of the early 1980s as part of that time period. I suppose the assured business of armaments carried on by Canadian Arsenals would help to explain why it ranked number three among the profit makers of the country. The Government expects the profits of the corporation of Canadian Arsenals Limited to grow and sales are expected to double over the next five years. There is a backlog of orders at the moment of some $200 million. What we have, then, is a Crown corporation which makes money. It is a Crown corporation which is profitable. But we have long since realized that when Conservatives look at Crown corporations, they assume that the profitable ones should be turned over to the private sector wherever that can be done so that the profits can be
privatized. The unfortunate money losers, or those Crown corporations which cannot realize a profit for reasons of public policy, we subsidize deliberately. The Conservatives always see these money losers as inevitably in the public's hands. There is this contrast between the privatization of profit and the socializing of poverty, of money losing. The capitalist Government, in the guise of this supposed Progressive Conservative Government, is very nicely practised in that. There can be no doubt that the Government is working on that kind of ideological principle even though there is a case for munitions manufacture, given the necessity of certain defence forces in our country, to be operating as a Crown corporation with limited profits going to the Government and where the Government is in fact in control.
This matter of control is not a feature to be glossed over lightly. Canada prides itself on controlling the sale of munitions as far as a number of trouble spots in the world are concerned. And, even more broadly, Canada prides itself on not selling munitions and weapons of war to countries which have human rights records of which we do not approve. We have, more or less, long lists of countries to which we would not sell weaponry, munitions and so on, even though my friend, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), pointed out last year that the Department of External Affairs appeared to be allowing the sale of certain material of this sort to Chile, one of the countries which has a thoroughly deplorable human rights record. Of course, these sales are made by enterprises whose only concern is to make a profit with no regard for how their products are used. Such sales exemplify very nicely the concern i feel in taking a useful enterprise-as long as we have defence forces in existence-and putting it into private hands beyond Government control so that they could do what they would with their product.
It distresses me that the press release of the Department of Supply and Services suggests at page 2 that:
SNC, in addition to offering the highest price, would substantially contribute towards making CAL an agent of growth and increased efficiency for the Canadian ammunition industry.
To have significant growth it is surely going to have to require sales outside of Canada. I think that is made quite clear on page 3 of the release where it states that:
As a Crown Corporation, CAL has been impeded in exploring opportunities to diversify. The Government is confident that once the company is privatized, CAL will pursue additional markets and product diversification.
It further states that:
-the Canadian ammunition industry should become internationally competitive.
It concludes with a reference to NATO sales. The reality is that NATO countries mostly have their own producers and are not very much in the market. There is far more danger that once CAL is owned by the SNC group in Montreal, it will be involved in producing and selling ammunition which might end up Lord knows where on the face of the earth. I believe that to mention this is justified because that other subsidiary to which I have already referred, IVI Incorporated, which was spun off in the mid-1960s, a producer of small calibre munitions, is
February 25, 1986

controlled by SNC, and in 1983 ammunition which had been produced by this company was in fact found in Nicaragua in the camps of the Contras who were carrying on their diabolical work of trying to overthrow the popular Government of the Sandinistas. The Contras have had a great deal of unofficial help from the United States and some help which gets perilously close to official. Surely, no Canadian Government, particularly given the stance taken by the Department of External Affairs in Central America, could approve of ammunition produced by IVI Incorporated ending up in the hands of the Contras. The merchants of death who operate these days in a number of other countries are desperately trying to obtain weapons and munitions, and there is considerable danger that Canadian Arsenals Limited will be found to be selling products to countries where Canadians generally would not want the products to be found. The loss of control over this industry is a very significant danger which follows as a consequence of the Government's decision to privatize profitable opportunity in munitions manufacture by getting rid of Canadian Arsenals Limited.
Surely, there are other unfortunate consequences in this proposal. The release to which I have referred with respect to exports states on page 3:
Significant efficiencies are expected to be achieved through joint efforts by CAL and IVI in such areas as administration, research and development, and marketing.
It is not difficult, surely, to appreciate that if IVI is involved in selling to the Department of National Defence, and has the organization to handle that, it can probably turf out some salesmen, some representatives and some people in administration after taking over CAL. When there are companies whose production is munitions there are certainly opportunities for efficiency but, surely, that means one thing only, and that is, a reduction in staff. The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Mclnnis) must expect that the result of disposing of CAL will be some loss of jobs, although we always find that these things are presented to us as being done for the sake of efficiency. But that should not cause us to close our eyes to the fact that here we will have a small addition to the unemployment rolls of the country-unemployment rolls which continue to grow despite the fact that the Government takes pride in the number of jobs that have been created. The Government of Canada should not be doing anything to add to the list of those who are unemployed. In fact, it should be doing the opposite. We should actively be trying to reduce the numbers. That is just one more of the flaws in the process which is before us.
It is also appropriate to comment on the way in which this situation was carried through in explaining our opposition to the proposal. In the Budget of last May 23 it became clear that the Government intended to dispose of Canadian Arsenals Limited. In the months following the Budget a process was undertaken which, according to a reporter of The Financial Post last December, left a good deal of bitterness in the Canadian business community, bitterness over the way in which it was carried through and ultimately with respect to the
Canadian Arsenals Limited
fact that only a small number of companies were in on the final competition. The reporter observed that the Department of Supply and Services does not have a great deal of experience in selling things and in divesting itself, or the Government, of assets such as this Crown corporation. That explanation strikes me as somewhat ingenuous because if the Department does anything, surely it does a good deal in terms of distributing on the part of the Government, certainly with respect to information and so on. However, I would concede that selling a Crown corporation is not the normal type of business for such a Department and so it would not be good at doing it.
One still wonders at the fact that the Department forced the potential buyers through three rounds of bidding, a process which surely cost a variety of companies a fair amount of money. The fact that the last six bidders were asked to compete in terms of price only reflected, on the one hand, the fact that these half a dozen companies were acceptable to the Government. I suppose it reflected, on the other hand, that here was something which was very desirable in terms of a money-making venture. In fact, it is as assured in terms of money-making as is baking bread or packing meat. After all, stuffing ammunition cases for the army is a pretty good business. So the Government was able to force as substantial a price as it could. Certain conditions were extorted as well from the successful buyer in terms of reassuring investment and ensuring that the company remains an efficient producer.
One of the most unfortunate irregularities about the whole situation is the fact that an employee, a Director General of aeronautics and ammunition purchases in the Department, suddenly left the Department in this period of time and moved to a consulting firm in Ottawa. This consulting firm was assisting SNC put its bid forward. Even though statements has been made about his not being involved with the process, surely that raises a question about the propriety of the whole process. If this particular employee did well in the process, then that is surely reason to be concerned about employees generally.
I have already suggested that efficiencies expected here can only be achieved at the cost of jobs. The fact that the Government carried the process through without any consultation with the workers and without any deliberation with the Public Service Alliance, which represents a large number of the workforce at Canadian Arsenals, is one more lamentable feature of the situation. We can only fear what will happen in the transition to private control as SNC takes over Canadian Arsenals Limited and conceivably forces a new organization to take over. Lord knows what else might happen in that particular area. This is just one more aspect of this unfortunate decision by Government which I decry this afternoon.
I suppose the only happy feature in the whole matter has to do with the fact that the Government is determined to ensure that once the Crown corporation is a private enterprise it will be Canadian controlled. That might give us some hope for the continuance of an economically successful enterprise. It also might give us some hope that the company will respect

February 25, 1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited
Canadian law and Canadian guidelines with respect to exports. This in spite of the fact that I have already alluded to IVI ammunition being found in Nicaragua, which means that even the assurance that it will be a Canadian-owned enterprise is no great assurance at all. It is satisfying to those of us who want opportunity for Canadian enterprise, if it cannot be done by Crown corporations. However, it is not a great deal of satisfaction.
I have been speaking in opposition to the measure this afternoon. I am not optimistic, of course, that our opposition will defeat the measure. When the measure comes before committee for careful consideration I expect that it will have the information available to it for a proper consideration of the matter before it is sent back to the House for third reading. The Andersen Report is particularly essential here. My last word on the subject is that this information has to be available to the committee in order for it to conduct a careful consideration of this proposal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want the Hon. Member to be misled. He made a point which I am sure he did not really mean to make. He said that he did not think the Department had experience in this type of venture, that is, with respect to sales, contracts, et cetera. I am sure he would agree that a Department which handles in excess of 300,000 contracts per year definitely has experience in sales, purchasing and contract negotiation. I am also sure he would agree that a Department which purchases or sells through Crown Assets Disposal Corporation close to $10 billion worth of products a year definitely has experience in those fields. I am sure he did not wish to mislead the House in that respect.
I am also sure that when he spoke about an employee who left the Department to go to a consulting firm which was associated with one of the bidders he was well aware that this person was close to retirement. As a good civil servant close to retirement he had feelers out to firms such as this one. When he recognized that there was a conflict of interest, he withdrew himself from all negotiations with the Department pertaining to the contract. He made a point of leaving the Department prior to any bids being received by any of the firms. He signed an agreement stating that he would not be involved in any way whatsoever with the contract. I am sure the Hon. Member would not want to cast a cloud on an ex-member of the Department who served his country so well.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that the Hon. Member was listening carefully to my remarks, so his first point is really superfluous. I conceded in my observations what he said, although since he has given me the occasion I will read the following sentence from The Financial Post of December 14, 1985. It reads:
The Government's handling of the sale .. . remains the source of much bitterness within the business community. Not least this was because the aims and objectives of the Department of Supply & Services-the agency responsible for the sale-were not always clear.
At least part of this is because DSS-which is the procurement arm for most government purchases, ranging from paperclips to jet fighters-is rather new at the game of selling government property to the private sector.
It is Mr. Bagnall whom I am quoting, and I too am inclined to think that DSS sells an awful lot of stuff and should know how to do it. Of course, selling a Crown corporation is not quite the same thing as disposing of government reports at exorbitant prices. In this case, we are all too likely to see Crown corporations sold off at a good deal less than that, and that might well reflect on the skill of the gentleman in charge of the Department of Supply and Services. 1 have no desire to reflect upon the officialdom in the Department in general. What I say does reflect, however, upon the Minister and his colleagues in Cabinet, of course, in appropriate style, given the way in which our Government functions.
As far as the second question is concerned, I would not want to reflect on the official who moved over. I will say in general, and I do not think he could object to this, that there is a real danger, and more than just the appearance of danger, when people leave a Department at a time as delicate as this and move into a consultancy business. If that consultancy business does not expect to get good value from this person, surely it will not take him in. It is not a matter of what he does not know about the bids that come in and how the Government reacts to them. What he does know is the way in which Government generally sees these things. I would think that it would be almost impossible for him to say anything about the Department without providing value to the consultancy firm.
The situation is not all that different, i think, from the situation of blind trusts that cabinet Ministers establish when they enter their offices and set aside their business involvements. Unless the trustee is given the power to deal freely and without informing the Minister of the holdings, I would think it would be difficult for a man who has been a sound and sensible investor-and I presume any Minister would be that if he had holdings that justified a blind trust-to forget his holdings. In those circumstances, it becomes almost impossible for a Minister who may possibly make a decision that relates to these holdings to not make a decision that will be to the benefit of his blind trust. Therefore, 1 think the only sensible way to go is to demand a period of at least a year in which there is a detachment from Government. I would not think that an official nearing retirement would forget all that much in a year, but presumably everything that was current would more or less have passed in that year's time and he could then move on without this same danger.
Without meaning to reflect on one particular official, because one should really reflect on others as well, if the general question is raised, I do not really want to take back my expression of concern about the appearance and what would be behind the appearance or underlie the concern about the appearance.
February 25, 1986

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a very short comment pertaining to that response. I am pleased to see a member of the New Democratic Party defending the business community and being so concerned about the Department upsetting the business community as was quoted from The Financial Post. Perhaps I could ask the Hon. Member if he has read the Auditor General's Report on the Department and if he is aware that the Auditor General has praised the activities and functioning of the Department in that area.
I would not want to belabour an issue such as the one of the civil servant in question, but that civil servant is an honourable one. He made an agreement that he would not be involved in activities with the Government for the required period. We acknowledge his honour. I do hope that he does not forget too much in the year because I am sure he will be of tremendous advantage to that firm in the future and I feel that more people who know how Government operates should become involved in consulting firms in Canada.
I congratulate this civil servant for moving over when he did and for being honourable enough to declare himself in conflict and divorce himself from the activities of the Department. I would not want to see a civil servant who retires being unable to be employed for a year. I think we can take civil servants at their word when they step aside and give their word that they will not be involved in Government operations.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to participate in the second reading debate on Bill C-87, an Act to authorize the sale of the Canadian Arsenals Limited. I listened with interest to the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) who addressed the issue very well from a number of different perspectives, including the consequences and perhaps repercussions of CAL being sold to a private firm, in this case the engineering group from Montreal, on the international scene.
I would like to touch on a number of other factors that concern the agreement to sell the Crown corporation to the engineering group from Montreal. By way of background, 1 think Canadians ought to know that this particular Crown corporation was established nearly 40 years ago and manufactures medium and large calibre ammunition. It operates two plants, one in Montreal which employs some 750 employees and another one near Quebec City employing somewhat fewer than 50 employees. Ninety per cent of its production is sold to the Department of National Defence and 10 per cent is exported to the international stage.
A number of different factors puzzle not only me but members of my Party and indeed constituents across the land. One of the things that seems incorrect about this deal is the secrecy surrounding it. The Government has made the decision to sell this particular Crown corporation to the engineering group from Montreal for a total price of some $92.2 million. Yet the Government's financial adviser in this deal has been Arthur Andersen Limited of Montreal. In questions in the House of Commons and in correspondence with the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Mclnnes), the Minister and the Government have refused very clearly to produce a copy of the
Canadian Arsenals Limited
financial report. They have refused to educate Canadians about the actual worth of this particular company in order that Canadians may be able to deduce that this particular selling price of some $92.2 million represents a good deal.
Canadians and we in Parliament are asking why there is this secrecy. Why is history repeating itself once again? By that, I am referring to the history of this Parliament. The Government has cloaked itself in a cocoon of secrecy before. When we were talking only a few short weeks ago of the de Havilland deal, it was difficult to pry any information out of the Government, information that was legitimately the prerogative of Canadians since they were the shareholders of de Havilland corporation. It was the same secrecy which was evident when we debated in the House for quite a stretch of time the bail-out of the two defunct banks only a few short months ago. we were being asked to sign a $1 billion cheque which was to go to invisible, unnamed, uninsured depositors with over $60,000 in their accounts. We in the House of Commons and Canadians in general were unable to obtain from the Government the information which was rightfully ours. We wanted to know who the depositors were so that we could determine where that large chunk of taxpayers' dollars would eventually land.
Was it a question which was somewhat too demanding? Was it a question which was inappropriate of Parliament and of Canadians? Of course it was not. It was information which should have been dealt with in a forthright and honest manner. Yet, one would think that after two lessons in public outcry the Government would somehow change its way of dealing with what is public property and public investment.
In respect of Canadian Arsenals Limited, we again have stonewalling and secrecy. Again we are told by the Government that we should just take its word for it that what it is doing is good for Canada. That worries me a great deal because I do not trust only the Government having the information, without sharing it with the Parliament of Canada and with Canadians. In fact, if it were such a great deal, knowing the public relations appetite of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney), they would be marching their troops across the country and advertising the greatness of the deal. They are not doing that. In fact, in a letter dated January 20 from the Minister of Supply and Services to the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Pre-scott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), the following was indicated: "I must once again advise you that I cannot provide you with a copy of the Arthur Andersen report. However, I can confirm that the Arthur Andersen company carried out a valuation study prior to commencement of the bidding and negotiating process and estimated the value range".
That is simply not good enough. We are talking about estimations. People want to know what the particular analysis produced. Why is the Government not prepared to table those results so that we may take the $92 million figure and compare it with the actual worth of the company? By itself, $92 million is worthless. A Canadian living in Downsview, Ontario could

February 25, 1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited
say that it is great that they got $92 million for it. However, an individual in Moose Jaw might say that it was terrible because they could have obtained $100 million. Who is to know the wide range of opinions that exist in the country? Why are Canadians being kept in the dark once again, if this is in fact such a great deal? That is one aspect with which we in this Party have problems. Following second reading and in committee, we will certainly pressure the Government and the Minister to make the information public and to provide Canadians with the backdrop upon which we can decide whether $92 million is a good deal or a bad deal.
The second question concerns the whole philosophy behind the sale of this particular Crown corporation. It does not make sense if one allows logic to follow its course. In the de Havilland corporation giveaway, because that is what it was, member after member of the government Party rose in his place and said that one of the major reasons for selling the corporation was that is was losing millions of dollars. They refused to look at all the other components. However, if we look at the central argument which they presented consistently and regularly, we have to wonder what were the criteria in respect of CAL. If we look at some of the figures, we see that CAL is very good from a financial perspective. Let us consider that from 1980 to 1985 it has consistently shown profits. In 1984-85 it showed profits of some $11.3 million. It has assets of over $126.4 million. It also has an accumulated total of $36 million in profits over the last few years. Therefore, one does not have to be a mathematician or an economist to understand that the Crown corporation was doing very well financially. Not only that, but sales in the next five years were projected to double. It also had $200 million in backlog orders.
Again Canadians and Parliamentarians are asking themselves: if on the one hand the de Havilland corporation was sold largely because it was losing money, why does the Government turn around a number of weeks or months later and sell a Crown corporation which is making money? What gives? What is the reasoning? What is the rationale? Where is the logic in Government policy? Where is the direction which the Government is attempting to provide? Where is consistent leadership? Where is consistent policy in respect of Crown corporations? Obviously the Government does not have one. One day it sells a Crown corporation because it is losing money. That is the reason given by Government Members. They boast, clap and cheer. Now they have a Crown corporation which is well operated financially and they do the same thing; they wish to sell it. That is inconsistent.
Another factor which is inconsistent is the philosophy which tries to understand why they wish to privatize one arm of Government which is supplying at a profit another arm of Government. Why toy with that interlinkage? Why toy with a network which is working within Government and supplying arms for the Canadian military? Why privatize one arm of Government which is serving another? It simply does not make sense. Individual Canadians are asking themselves, from a philosophical point of view at least, how the Government can rationalize decision-making in respect of two Crown corporations as we have seen in de Havilland and in Canadian Arsenals Limited.
Another factor is the consultation and tendering process in the sale of this corporation. If one reads the commentaries, there has been very little consultation. For instance, the Public Service Alliance of Canada, the union which many CAL employees fall under, indicated the following as its basic reason: "The Government never bothered to talk to the union about the deal". It also said: "We question the rationale of the Government selling a Crown corporation that does business only with the Government". Another quote was: "We feel that the Government will be in an uncomfortable position buying from a foreign company if CAL is not competitive". There has been little consultation in respect of the selling of this Crown corporation. Moreover, some bidders expressed a concern that the Department conducted the selling of this Crown corporation in an amateur fashion, that the Department of Supply and Services basically relied on word of mouth and contacted companies informally, in the end inviting six companies to place bids rather than making the process open and rather than making the process accountable and accessible to one and all. This is reminiscent of the sale of de Havilland when, right from the start, one company was strongly favoured over another company, which happened to be Canadian. Those are some of the questions which have not been answered at this stage of second reading. Those questions must be pursued vigorously, if not in the House of Commons during second reading, then at committee stage where the evidence of a number of expert witnesses will perhaps clarify the picture for us.
When one looks at the secrecy and the inconsistency of the Government within a span of two to three months with regard to Crown corporations, one must wonder where the Government is going, where it wants to take Canadians, and what message it wants to leave with them. It is no wonder that Canadians are questioning the leadership of this administration. The Prime Minister was successful in attaining his office, but when he got to 24 Sussex he said: "Where do we go from here? What now?"
During the last federal election campaign the Prime Minister campaigned on a commitment of opening up Government, making it more accessible, and providing more information to Canadians to enable them to see how the Government is functioning on their behalf. Where are those commitments now? Where is the information? Where was the information on the de Havilland sale? Where was the information with respect to the bank bail-outs and the uninsured depositors?

lauded for making a great deal, and I would stand in my place and say so. However, if Arthur Andersen had suggested that the value of that Crown corporation was greater than $92 million, we would know that the Conservative Government is trying to hide its embarrassment.

speechtext:
that Bill C-257, an Act respecting the conservation, export and diversion of water resources, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, you may ask why this Bill is being introduced so I will briefly explain. With the consent of the Government, which I hope will allow it to go through, this Bill will ensure that Parliament has the final word should Cabinet decide one day, perish the thought, in favour of a diversion or export of our water. The possibility of this happening did not exist until recently. The unfortunate interview given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to Fortune magazine some time ago, along with the $30,000 grant which the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) gave to the Grand Canal company, has given credibility and momentum to something which, under normal circumstances, was considered a crackpot idea, and quite rightly so. I would not want it thought that this measure is generated simply because of the Grand Canal proposal. It is because of the possibility that water diversion and export may really emerge on the political agenda of Canada in the decades to come. This Bill attempts to bring the issue forward for examination by this and future Parliaments in order that a specific decision related to water exports is not made by Cabinet alone.
You may ask why this matter needs to be addressed by way of a Bill, and why it does not amend an existing Act. The reason is simply that no such legislation exists because, until

February 25, 1986
Water Export and Diversion Act
now, we have never seen the need of introducing such legislation. As 1 mentioned a moment ago, the possibility never emerged as something which should be addressed seriously. However, in recent months it has become more than a possibility, and that causes some of us enormous concern. Therefore, we feel the necessity for putting forward a parliamentary proposal, Bill C-257, for the consideration of this House.
By way of contrast with the interview that the Prime Minister had with Fortune magazine, I would like to quote Prime Minister St. Laurent who had this to say about water export policy in 1947:
Can we, in fairness to Canadian generations of the future, allow such natural wealth to be diverted from our own territory and put to uses from which it would be extremely difficult afterwards to withdraw it?
Those words are as much the reality today as they were more than 40 years ago, and perhaps even more so.
In essence this Bill makes the point that political, social, economic and environmental values are affected when it comes to permitting the diversion and export of water. From a political point of view, if we were to embark on a major diversion of our water, it would mean that we would integrate this continent's water resources. This would inevitably, in my opinion, lead to political integration. I would like to quote General McNaughton when he warned in 1966:
-if we make a bargain to divert water to the United States we cannot ever discontinue or we will face force to compel compliance.
Once you divert, Mr. Speaker, you create a dependency. Once you divert, you cannot turn the tap off. Once you divert, the political hand of the stronger partner is the one which really has the power to turn the tap off, if it can be turned at all.
I would also like to put forward some thoughts of a social nature as it affects possible diversions, particularly that which has been speculated upon recently concerning the Hudson Bay area. Here the social consequences would be felt by our native people. It would affect their lifestyle. It would affect their ability to live in the environment to which they are accustomed. The flow of rivers would be reversed or otherwise diverted. Pumping stations in considerable numbers would have to be installed. The cultural dislocation that would follow would be very hard to describe, and the native people have expressed on a variety of occasions their strong opposition to any diversion of this kind. Another social impact which is important to mention would be the effect diversion would have on agriculture in the decades to come. A large segment of Canadian society whose activity depends on water would be affected if we were to make the changes which some proponents, presently subsidized by this Tory Government, are putting forward in their studies and sketchy proposals.
Another concern has to do with the economy. As we are endowed with such a wealth of water in Canada, we would be wise to ask ourselves whether we should use that water to attract investment rather than to have it used by other countries. 1 respectfully submit that it would be in our interest to use the water to add economic value here at home rather than to export it and allow other countries to add value to a very
important and basic commodity. In addition, some of us still need to be convinced that Canada's hydro exports are really such a big bargain considering that hydro rates do not, and I repeat, do not take into account the capital and construction investments. If we were to export water we would face a situation whereby fresh water would be going abroad and we would have to use in Canada, perhaps, recycled water because of the arrangements to which we were committed, and, perhaps because of increased necessities and demand at home, which we would not be able to meet in the long term, because of the commitments made in the export and diversion of water.
On the environmental side there are several considerations that one must keep in mind. We have Canadian needs that will be determined by population growth, by the greenhouse effect and by the shift of agriculture perhaps to more northern latitudes when the predicted greenhouse effect will occur. In the second half of the next century the meteorologists are predicting an increase in temperature of some 2 to 3 degrees centigrade. That means that the present geography of our agriculture will likely move further north and we may see some areas of Canada become unuseable in terms of agricultural activity. As a result of increased average annual temperature there might be an increase in the consumption of water, and not just for agricultural purposes but also for normal human consumption.
Another environmental consideration is that when the water is diverted and exported, that water becomes part of another ecosystem. It becomes used in another ecosystem and becomes part of that water system to which it has been exported or diverted. That may have some consequences on the climate and the operations in that particular area. It is quite possible that diverted and exported water that goes into another ecosystem will have, in the long term, consequences on both regions; the one that has lost the water and the one that has obtained the water.
Then there is the physical removal of water, which in the case of Hudson's Bay, as it is suggested in the proposal 1 mentioned earlier, would lead to increased salinity of the bay because the fresh water rivers would no longer discharge into Hudson's Bay, but that water would be pumped up in the opposite direction. Therefore, the benefit of fresh water going into Hudson's Bay would be reduced considerably, thus increasing the salt content of that immense and magnificent water body. There would be changes in the availability of nutrients, of course. There would be an impoverished wetland system downstream. There could also be some considerable changes in the ice formation in that region with concomitant effects on wildlife, not to mention the impact on the immediate environment that would take place by way of the construction of reservoirs, dams, canals, power stations and the like.
In addition to that, another real concern is that when you propose to reverse the flow of rivers, as is the case in Hudson's Bay, what you would do is to stir up the sediments in the bottom of each of these rivers, and in the areas that are heavily
February 25, 1986

industrialized, or which have collected sediments coming from industrial areas, you would be stirring up toxic chemicals which have, over time, settled in the sediments of these river beds. Thus you would cause considerable disturbances and probably affect the quality of water for some years at least. The long-term effects of divergence can only be measured decades later. It is, as we all know from experiences made in some countries, irreversible in nature.
That brings me then to the purpose of this Bill which, in essence, is determined by the restrictions imposed on us backbenchers as to what one can put into a Bill. In this particular instance the scope available to me as a back-bencher was restricted by rules, by which we all abide, and therefore you will find in this Bill an attempt to make it as difficult as possible to approve water diversions or exports. That is where my bias emerges inevitably and quite willingly. The Bill not only makes it as difficult as possible to approve water diversion and exports, but also the proponent has to carry the burden of proof, and he has to prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that this proposal would be in the absolute long-term interest of Canadians.
The approach through this Bill is quite different from the one we are now witnessing outside this chamber when a company called the Grand Canal can come forward and obtain money from the Government and where the Financial burden of proving that a proposal is good or bad is not really at stake. The proponent is giving funds to demonstrate that this proposal is sound. I find this concept so offensive that I cannot express it in words.
There may be some objections by people who will ask, "Why deny business the opportunity to make money with water?" Of course the answer to that is fairly straightforward, and that is, because water is a public good, and because no one has a claim to ownership of water except the public. In the end this is one of the common properties, such as air and soil, that we have over centuries and millenia learned to appreciate as an important component in sustaining life on this globe. To reinforce these concepts on water exports and on water diversions I will quote Clause 6(3). It reads:
(a)	the ability of available water supplies to meet long-term Canadian requirements;
(b)	the impact of water export on fisheries, navigation, federal waters and international waters;-
And that applies also to diversions. It continues to read:
(c)	the impact of water export or diversions on the interests of native groups and others and the adequacy of compensation to them for any adverse effects;
(d)	the ecological and economic advantages and disadvantages to Canada of water exports; and
(ie) the political and strategic impact of water export.
Having put forward those criteria I hope that I can call on the Minister to consider this Bill only as a step forward in the Government's political determination to create a national water board and, in the meantime, to adopt the principle expounded in the Pearse Report that water should be managed and kept within its watershed.
Water Export and Diversion Act
I conclude by quoting from that report on page 8, where the Commissioners say:
The watershed is the natural and most appropriate unit for water management. A federal water policy that will ensure Canadians sufficient safe water to sustain their physical, economic and social well-being for all time is desirable.
This is the main intent I am putting forward through Bill C-257.
