speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I simply confirm that it is on page 4276 of Hansard. I believe I expressed both the tone and the exact words accurately.
In any event, this is an issue of vital importance and a topic that should be seriously considered by Canadians. I am grateful to the Hon. Member for Davenport for giving us this opportunity to discuss it.
Furthermore, if we are going to claim accuracy, 1 think it would be fair for the Hon. Member for Davenport to attribute authorship and support for some of the water diversion

February 25, 1986
Water Export and Diversion Act
schemes to members of the Liberal Party who have espoused them, as is the case. The Hon. Member should consider that when talking about accuracy and the Conservative proposals.
Water, like the rest of our natural environment, is vitally integrated into the economic structure of our country and the health of our citizens. It is an excellent example of the inter-dependency of our environment and our economy.
Our sometimes almost casual view of water is reflected in the consideration of exports. In fact, water is exported every day, as is agricultural produce, processed food, bottled water, beer, which the Hon. Member for Davenport and I occasionally share, paper and a multitude of other exports from raw resource to finished produce, to say nothing of fish and electricity.
For the record, there is no doubt that Canada is one of the have nations of the world with respect to the abundance of its fresh water resources. However, it may not be clear to many Canadians or to the Hon. Member, considering some of his comments, what our favoured position is with respect to fresh water.
Our ground water situation is not as well understood as in many other countries, largely because we have relied so much on surface resources. Canada probably has more lake area than any other country in the world. Large and small, these surface waters dot the landscape from one end of the country to the other.
Valuable as they are in regulating the flow of rivers to the sea, and in providing a rich habitat for natural life and human enjoyment, Canadian lakes are for the most part a one-time gift of glacial recession. They are not renewable, except at a cost to the rivers that feed and drain them. The best measure of a country's water supply, therefore, is its renewable river flow originating from surface sources and including ground water contributions.
On an average annual basis, Canada's rivers carry close to 9 per cent of the world's renewable water supply, which is roughly 100,000 cubic metres per second. Set against a Canadian population which is less than 1 per cent of the world's population, this is a generous endowment. If we set this against a territorial area encompassing about 7 per cent of the world's land mass, this is not so disproportionate. In any event, this figure of 9 per cent is far less than the 20 per cent to 40 per cent often attributed to Canada.
The Hon. Member for Davenport touched on the federal inquiry. The federal inquiry on water policy which the Member for Davenport was instrumental in establishing, reported to the Government in September, 1985. It did an excellent job in bringing the linkages between water uses, water quality and quantity issues, and between engineering, economic, social, environmental and constitutional aspects to the attention of the lay public and even to water resource experts across Canada.
One of the very valid points the inquiry has made is that policies relating to water overlap and interact. "Take up one and you have to take up the others".
The report made many specific observations, and one to which the Hon. Member's Bill draws attention is the difference in water exports. The Hon. Member's Bill indicates that he is considering both southward diversions and other forms of export as being subject to licensing by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) with provisions for revocation of the ministerial permits by Parliament. The proposed Bill differentiates between tankers or forms of container shipment to some overseas countries or perhaps to some U.S. port and large scale diversion via dedicated facilities such as canals, pipelines or river routes to the United States.
This distinction is clearly justifiable. Tanker exports differ from inter-basin diversions in substantial ways. For example, the volumes would likely be small, exports would be sporadic and importers are not likely to become dependent upon Canadian water as in the case of large scale inter-basin diversions. The Pearce Report identified these matters very clearly for all of us.
Accordingly, it may be argued that the federal Government could be more flexible in terms of tanker exports provided that federal interests such as fisheries and navigation are not affected and that the Crown receives a fair return for water exported in this fashion.
However, the question arises: What new legislation to control and regulate such exports do we need, or could existing legislation such as the Export and Import Act be amended to regulate water along with other commodities on its list?
However, in consideration of other water exports, what municipal and provincial if not international considerations must be taken? We must also ask ourselves if the acceptance of containerized water exports would encourage proponents of large scale diversions to press their case to Governments increasingly. It would seem that the Hon. Member for Davenport anticipates this to be the case and has already set out some basic criteria for export by diversion, canal and pipelines within the statutory framework outlined in his Bill.
Let me now in the time remaining lay out for the House the important rationale for the management of Canadian waters by the Conservative Government of Canada. First and foremost is the need for a Canadian national water policy, and this is a goal and commitment of the Government of Canada today. In releasing publicly the final report of the inquiry on federal water policy last September 30, the Minister of the Environment declared that this was only the first step in policy reform. He stated:
Water issues are not yet at the crisis stage, and we will be able to manage them co-operatively if we start today to work toward a national consensus, or a national water policy.
The Government's response to the federal inquiry has been rapid and constructive. The Government accepts this document as an important background in establishing the necessary elements of a national water policy. Within one week we requested the provincial Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers to respond at a meeting of CCREM,
February 25, 1986

and that will be included in the agenda of the next CCREM meeting. In November, the Minister met and discussed the report with representatives of 300 or so environmental nongovernment organizations. Both provincial and public interests have been invited to join in the response to the inquiry's recommendation so that the resulting consensus areas can form the nucleus of a nationally applicable policy on water.
Second, at the federal Government level, leadership and responsibility must be defined and taken. One problem which has been identified with respect to this whole issue is that we have not had that clear responsibility taken and acted upon in the past. That now has been done. In December of 1985, at a meeting of the Priorities and Planning Committee of Cabinet, the Minister of the Environment was empowered to act for the Government in formulating a national water policy. The Minister now has the authority to act for Canadians in all matters relating to water. The Minister is giving first priority to a national water policy. There will be no decision for or against large-scale water exports or other water issues until these issues can be weighed in context of the over-all water policy.
Third, the Progressive Conservative federal Government has clearly stated-and this has been confirmed several times by several Ministers in the House of Commons-that water exports are not-I repeat, are not-an item of negotiation during the current bilateral trade negotiations with the United States. As Hon. Members know, the news media have linked the question of water export to the discussions on freer trade with the United States. I am sure that the House has read the statement by Canada's chief negotiator, Mr. Simon Reisman, that while he holds strong personal views on water exports, those views are not relevant to his role of chief trade negotiator. That was a statement made by Mr. Reisman which was published in The Ottawa Citizen on January 24, 1986. This reaffirms statements by Ministers of the Government that water exports are not now on the negotiating table.
Consideration of large-scale exports of water would involve provinces, states and the Canadian and United States Governments. We would have to consider the rights and obligations of all Parties, compensation for lands, disruption of existing services and actual and potential environmental damages. I believe some of the problems which might be encountered were well defined by the Hon. Member opposite, and these issues will clearly have to be considered if anyone were even to start out on this long process.
I must also mention a point I believe the Hon. Member for Davenport has missed. Anyone who would seriously entertain a project of this type right now would have to have his head buried in the economic sand because if anyone looks at the actual costs of any type of major diversion, particularly the Grand Canal diversion, he would find that the cost is so prohibitive as to make the project totally uneconomical. At this point I do not have the reference here but I believe those figures are readily available to anyone and can certainly be provided.
Finally, the Grand Canal proposal mentioned by the Hon. Member has been around for many years. This or any other
Water Export and Diversion Act proposal of this type can only be considered, in our opinion, in the context of what would be a national formulated water policy. In other words, whether or not anything like this in the future could occur is irrelevant at this time and will not even be entertained by the Government of Canada until we have developed what we feel is the national water policy with all the aforementioned considerations.
Various agencies inside or outside of Government may wish to investigate any number of things, one on which the Hon. Member has focused, but none of these activities will prejudice our intention to establish a national water policy with full consideration of all implications of water issues on behalf of all Canadians.
I have not touched at all on other water related issues. I think many of the same points I have made in terms of water exports could be made in terms of other water issues, some of them pretty overwhelming right now, such as the spill in the St. Clair River, toxic substances in the Niagara River, and dumps which have to be dealt with. All of these other issues are issues of water quality and would be better dealt with in the context of a national water policy. However, they are overwhelmingly important now and must be dealt with as quickly and as well as possible with the tools at hand.
I will not spend a long time in trying to reaffirm the efforts and initiatives we have taken so far as water quality itself is concerned. I hope in the near future that we will be able to deal with the aspect of water quality, but clearly all of the water issues as they overlap and interrelate can be best dealt with in the context of a national water policy and under the responsibility of a single Minister. These are things which are coming together in a very rapid and, I believe, very constructive fashion. They will help to overcome some of the difficulties we have in dealing with different Departments and different pieces of legislation which are clearly inadequate in the face of our modern-day problems.
What I have done as clearly as possible is to define the leadership and responsibility we have taken. Hon. Members can refer to the record to examine the three major points I made. However, I think in the end, they must relegate any question of exports, diversions and other high profile issues to a very secondary position in terms of real priorities. In the context of a national water policy, issues like that can be considered.
One of the specific issues raised by the critic for the Liberal Party is the carbon dioxide level. I would suggest that some of his technical considerations are not quite accurate and I would invite him to check on those. He is quite right in terms of agricultural activity heading north, but the two things I believe he could check on are the water content which will be in those northern lands and what will really happen in the river basins and in the water levels. I am not positive but I will ask him to check those things because from what I could hear and understand him saying, I do not believe he was clearly stating what I think will happen with the carbon dioxide increase.
The second point I would make is in terms of priorities and real issues as he and I sit in this House of Commons today. I

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to have an opportunity to participate in this debate today on behalf of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), who unfortunately cannot be here to speak to Bill C-257.
I have some grave reservations about Bill C-257. I do not have grave reservations about the position of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), since I know he is sincere when he says that his intention is to find ways to prevent major water diversions and exports. My concern with Bill C-257 is that it is at once a road map to sell Canada dry, while at the same time it sets up a steeplechase-not a simple act to expedite exports of water. My preference would have been to have either the Hon. Member or other Members of the House bring forward a national water Act which would keep water, as the Hon. Member has said, within its own watershed and within its own ecological regime. I will spend the majority of my time this afternoon dealing with that from a scientific perspective from the information I wish to put on the record.
I would first like to place a few matters before Hon. Members. First, Canada has 1 per cent of the world's population while having 9 per cent of the world's freshwater supply. Some 60 per cent of our freshwater flows northward, while about 90 per cent of Canadians live along or just south of the 49th parallel. The United States has ten times our population and 8 per cent of the world's freshwater supply. However, almost all of it, according to American scientists, is mismanaged or polluted. That is really the problem in the United States today. Water is becoming a far more critical commodity than energy. There is no longer any such thing as free water.
Exporting water to the United States will dramatically reduce the likelihood of any action by that country to cut back on S02, N02 or other airborne pollutants, particularly from coal-fired thermal plants and other producers in the United States. Similarly, it will likely reduce the likelihood of the United States cleaning up its toxic dumps, such as the S area
dump, Hyde Park, Love Canal and others which are polluting both Canadian and American water supplies. We know we have already lost thousands of lakes in Ontario and Quebec and tens of thousands are threatened with acidification from airborne pollutants. We see no serious sign of use in the United States of the super fund to clean up its toxic dumps which contain such things as dioxin which are getting into the freshwater supplies of both our countries. That was brought forward by the Humboldt-Lake Centre NDP Association.

The constancy of earth's water supply is one of nature's great wonders. Our water molecules do not fly apart into hydrogen and oxygen, they don't flee our atmosphere into space, they don't slither down deep-earth crevices. Virtually all the water on earth-about 326 million cubic miles of it-has been present as liquid, ice, or vapor since it spewed out of countless volcanoes 3 billion years ago and more. And all of it, whether trapped a dark mile deep in Antarctic ice of drifting high and fast as a particle of cloud, is part of the vast, complex machine called the hydrologic cycle.
This machine, by far the world's largest, is powered by the sun. Solar energy provides enough heat to evaporate about 140,000 cubic miles of water a year: the same amount returns to the earth's surface as precipitation.

She said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to outline the Government's borrowing requirements for the upcoming fiscal year. I want to begin by paraphrasing the remarks made by my most honourable colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), when he presented the previous borrowing Bill before this Chamber last May. At that time he said that he could garner little enthusiasm in bringing forward such a measure, a measure dealing with a legacy of the previous administration and which imposed an extraordinary severe burden on the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform Hon. Members that I share my colleague's lack of enthusiasm for this measure which we tabled last May. However, I am confident that the credible, honest and praiseworthy document the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled Wednesday afternoon represents a firm extension of his commitment and this Government's commitment to remedy the sad state of affairs that we inherited.

The evidence is before us today. This Bill is testimony to the sound progress that this Government has made. I am sure all Hon. Members are aware that our borrowing needs, thanks to my colleague the Minister of Finance, have been reduced from $28.8 billion last year to $22.6 billion this year. That is a full $6.2 billion less. Furthermore, as my colleague the Minister of Finance told us yesterday, our borrowing needs will continue to be reduced every year thereafter.
On September 4, 1984, Canadians voted overwhelmingly for a new approach to the way this country is governed. Three months later the Minister of Finance presented to the House his economic statement, a historic document, which outlined an agenda of economic renewal and set out the principles and new policy directions designed to clear the way for sustained growth and to create permanent jobs at low, stable rates of inflation.
Hon. Members will recall that the three major challenges he identified at that time were: restoring fiscal integrity, encouraging private initiative, and redefining the role of Government so that it provides an effective framework for economic growth and job creation. On May 23 last year the Minister built on this comprehensive economic strategy and presented us with a Budget designed to redress high unemployment and spiralling national debt. This past Wednesday we were given the proposals of his current Budget, proposals which are consistent with and complementary to those of his previous addresses to this House.
Today, in bringing before the Chamber a Bill to authorize the Government's planned borrowing requirements for the forthcoming year, I want to underscore the fact that the consistent and comprehensive application of the strategy which
was first enunciated a year ago last November and developed in the May 1985 Budget, a strategy built on prudent management and good, old fashioned common sense, has produced results. This success can clearly be seen in the renewed optimism in Canada and in the jobs that have been created and the consumer confidence which is at its highest level in many years. The Government is putting the nation back together by promoting growth, creating jobs, improving Government effectiveness and controlling our national debt. This is the first Government in many years that has had the discipline and sense of stewardship to do this.
This is a clear demonstration of the leadership and initiative displayed by Progressive Conservatives, by the people on this side of the House and by the Government. We have acted with decisiveness, with consistency, with determination, with discipline and with a sense of responsibility. We as a nation cannot continue to mortgage our future. Therefore, we are taking the actions that we have to take. We are restraining the Government's needs to make sure that, like all other Canadians, we are spending smarter. Canadians are tired of having their futures mortgaged as well as their homes.
The Minister of Finance said very clearly last May that at some point we must begin to pay the bills for current services and not pass them on to our children. We as a Government are determined to put our fiscal house in order. When independent comparisons and studies are made with other countries, it becomes very clear that we are succeeding in this resolve. Between 1982 and 1984, Canada recorded the largest deficit among the major OECD countries with the exception of Italy. With the measures that have been brought forward by this Government, the deficit will decline from 6.3 per cent of GNP in 1984 to 4.7 per cent in 1986. This represents the largest decline, along with Japan, among the seven OECD countries. That is a record of which we are going to be very proud.
[Translation[
We are on the way to new economic prosperity. However, 1 would not want Hon. Members to think this Government will rest on its laurels. The economic problems still facing our country are not easy to resolve. To attain our Government's objective of full economic recovery will require a sustained effort on the part of all Members of this House, and I earnestly ask you to support us in this very important task. [English]
Let me turn now to the specifics of the Bill before the House. The Bill seeks $22.6 billion worth of borrowing authority for 1986-87, an amount exactly equal to the forecast financial requirements for the year, and no additional amount of borrowing authority is being sought at this time. I should explain that a new borrowing authority Bill would normally include an amount equivalent to the financial requirements and a specified amount for contingencies such as possible foreign exchange requirements. This year, the Government has recourse to $2 billion of unused non-lapsing authority which was provided by the Borrowing Authority Act, 1984-85, (No. 2). Thus, no contingency amount is being required.
February 28, 1986

To remain consistent from one year to the next, Clause 3 of the Bill stipulates that all unused borrowing authority granted by this Bill or by the Borrowing Authority Act, 1984-85, (No. 2) to the extent that the unused authority exceeds $2 billion will be cancelled. Thus, any unused borrowing authority remaining from the $2 billion non-lapsing amount granted earlier will be cancelled at the end of the fiscal year and may not be carried forward again. The provision to cancel all unused authority granted for the 1986-87 fiscal year to the extent that it exceeds $2 billion is similar to previous years and if available will preserve a $2 billion non-lapsing amount to be carried forward into the 1987-88 fiscal year.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, in May 1985, the Minister of Finance tabled a paper proposing improvements to the Canadian budgetary process. One of the suggestions in that paper was to seek parliamentary approval of borrowing authority for the upcoming fiscal year at the same time the Budget was presented. The logic behind the proposal is really self-evident. It is that the Budget presentation in February would set out the financial information for the new fiscal year for parliamentary study, and this is the course of action that I am following now. I would hope that the debate on the Budget and the fiscal stance presented by the Government will be helpful in the examination of the borrowing authority Bill.
As a matter of interest to Hon. Members, I would like to outline how the Government has made use of the borrowing authority provided by Parliament for the 1985-86 fiscal year. The total amount of authority provided was $32.2 billion. It consisted of $12 billion provided by the borrowing Authority Act 1985-86; $18.2 billion provided by the Borrowing Authority Act, 1985-86, (No. 2); and a $2 billion non-lapsing reserve carried forward from the Borrowing Authority Act, 1984-85, (No. 2). During the 1985-86 fiscal year to date, domestic borrowing operations have used about $23 billion of borrowing authority, $7.3 billion through the issue of treasury bills, $11.4 billion through the sale of marketable bonds and $4.3 billion through the net sale of Canada Savings Bonds.
There was in addition foreign borrowing that added $8.2 billion to the use of borrowing authority. The foreign borrowing represented a $900 million U.S. public issue in the U.S. market in July, a $500 million bond issue in the Eurodollar market in November 1985, a $80 billion public bond issue in the Euro-yen market in February 1986 and a U.S. $1 billion bond issue in the Eurodollar market in February 1986. In addition, net standby drawings during the 1985-86 fiscal year to date have used $4 billion of borrowing authority. There was also a redemption of a U.S. $250 million public issue in October which reduced the total use of borrowing authority. The borrowing authority calculations reflect as well the repayment of portions of Canadair financial corporation debt that was assumed by the Government in the 1985-86 fiscal year.
Let me close my remarks by urging the House to effect swift passage of the legislation that is before us today. Hon. Members I am sure will recall that last May, the borrowing Bill was debated within two weeks of the Budget. This year we are debating it within two days.
Borrowing Authority Act
We are discussing this measure in the light of Wednesday's Budget, and I shall be happy to hear any comments that Hon. Members may wish to make on this very important matter, Mr. Speaker.

I am reminded of a quotation from Hippocrates: "Healing is a matter of time, but it is also a matter of opportunity". 1 ask all Hon. Members to seize the opportunity offered to us this week by the Minister of Finance, the opportunity to build a better future for Canada. 1 also ask Hon. Members to pass this Bill rapidly enough to allow us to stay the course we charted in November, 1984 which has been so successful in our economic environment to date, so that we can once again restore the nation to its potential.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1986-87 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the borrowing authority Bill introduced by the Government after its first Budget last May requested over $18 billion. This was after the presentation of a Budget which was and is widely perceived as an outright attempt by the Government to tax its way out of the deficit at the expense of middle and low-income Canadians.
Today we are considering another request for borrowing authority. Again the Government has presented a Budget which is very little more than across-the-board regressive tax increases, except that they will hit doubly hard, since the new increases are piled on to those already in effect from the last Budget, and again middle-income Canadians are hit. And yet, with this double whammy effect, with the further squeeze which the Government is putting on average taxpayers, the Bill before us requests no less than $22.6 billion for 1986-87.
What kind of questions does this raise about the way the Government has chosen to proceed in its two Budgets and the way it has governed in the time it has been in power? We in the Official Opposition opposed many of the measures in last year's Budget because of their unfairness. The broadening of the sales tax base, sales tax increases and deindexation are measures which impact upon everyone, but hit hardest at families and individuals with low and moderate incomes. We have pointed out repeatedly as the budget Bills came before the House that the sales and excise taxes have a multiplier effect which enhances their unfairness. Year after year they will take bigger and bigger bites from the incomes of taxpayers. Their effect is only beginning to be felt. The billions of dollars the Government takes in this year through the tax hikes in last year's Budget alone will multiply several times by the end of the decade.
With concerted effort from the Opposition and strong protest from Canadians in general, we were able to force the Government to change some of its most damaging proposals. The Government backed off from its plan to strip inflation

February 28, 1986
Borrowing Authority Act
protection from old age pensions, and the Government restored the sales tax exemption for certain medical supplies.
The unfairness of the Conservative Government's first Budget was highlighted by the treatment afforded to large corporations and to the small minority of wealthy Canadians. While middle and low-income Canadians got all the rough treatment in the Budget, those groups were left relatively unscathed: in fact, one might say that they got off better than unscathed.
In contrast to the loss of protection against inflation, the deindexation of the personal tax system and the tax grabs perpetrated upon low and middle-income earners, the fortunate 4 per cent of the population who can afford it, were given the gift of a $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption. There were no strings attached, no restrictions, no requirement that investments qualifying for the exemption contribute in any way to building our economy. It is simply an unsolicited, untargeted bonus which further complicates the tax system.
It is important to remember these things about the Government's Budget of last year because we are living with these measures right now. I certainly agree with the Minister of Finance and other Government supporters who say that we must consider the two Budgets as a package. We in the Official Opposition were and are against measures adopted by the Government in its first Budget last year. We did not believe then and we do not believe now that the way to cut the deficit is by taxing the life and spirit out of middle and low-income Canadians. We urged the Government to take the opportunity in its second Budget to repair some of the damage done in its first Budget. We urged the Government to modify the capital gains exemption, to add some conditions. We urged the Government to address the fact that its measures were creating a gap between the "haves" and "have-nots" in society. We urged the Government to introduce measures which would show us that it had a vision and an agenda for economic growth.
The Official Opposition was not the only voice encouraging the Government to such action. Many other groups and individuals also encouraged it to bring about a fair and an imaginative Budget-groups from social policy organizations, to business groups, to individual citizens. However, on February 26 it became clear that the Government had not listened. On February 26 Canadians got more of the same-more tax increases, more hidden tax changes.
The speeches which I gave during last year's debate on the Budget and last year's debate on the borrowing authority Bill are quite relevant today and could almost be applied verbatim to this year's debates. We have now had two Budgets which have taken exactly the same stance, to wring as much as possible in tax revenues from middle and low-income Canadians in an effort to cut the deficit and to prove to outside investors that the Conservative Government has the ability and resolve to manage our economy. It may be early to judge the international reaction, but the dollar has dropped on each of the two days since the Budget was presented. It will probably be another couple of weeks before we know what international
investors think of a Government which in two successive Budgets latches on and clings to the method of raising revenue by taxing and then taxing some more. Will that be a signal that the Government has a vision of where it wants the country
to go?
Reaction to the $500,000 capital gains exemption with no strings attached was lukewarm at best, negative in large part, but there has been no move to modify it. I think the Minister would have acquired great credit if he had been willing to admit that that was a mistake and to add in some conditions so that people who benefit from such a measure would contribute to the Canadian economy in some way. However, he chose not to do so.
On top of the 1 per cent federal sales tax increase in the last Budget, this Budget now gives us another 1 per cent increase on all items including gasoline. We should remember that because fuel costs are a part of all manufacturing, packaging, transportation, storage and retailing, any increase in fuel costs means higher prices for the consumer.
This measure is only one of the many measures in this Budget which are inflationary. Canadians will have to dig deeper into their pockets to pay a further $1.9 billion in federal taxes while corporate taxes increase by only $380 million.
As a result of the Conservative Government's two budgets, middle and low-income Canadians will have less money because of higher taxes, and they must use their reduced incomes to buy goods that are made more expensive because of higher taxes.
The small compensations offered in the February 26 budget do not come close to compensating for what Canadians are losing through these repeated tax grabs. The so-called federal sales tax rebate will be a help to some poor Canadians, but it will be a pittance compared to what they will lose over the years because of the cumulative effects of deindexation and tax increases.
As for the proposal to give some low income families their child tax credit a few months early, it is beyond me how that can be presented by the Government as generosity. The Government is patting itself on the back for offering to give people the money it owes them.
These are the two measures Government Members are pointing to as proof of the Conservative Government's compassion and sense of fairness. I would simply point out that they are small and very inexpensive measures which will be paid for several times over by what the Government expects to rake in with the 3 per cent surtax.
It remains to be seen if this concerted attack on the middle class will have the effect the Government wanted. It will raise revenue, but the Government also hopes it will convince international investors of its determination to manage the economy. This brings me to a concern I raised earlier. Dr. Lehr, a geology professor at Ohio State University, was introduced as the foremost U.S. expert on ground water.

Dr. Lehr said farmers use irrigation methods which use only about 35 per cent of the water on crops, wasting the other two-thirds.
Vested interests ensure that the United States consumes more surface water, from lakes, streams and rivers, than ground water from beneath the earth's surface, although there is 20 times more ground water in storage than there is surface water, he said.
Engineers get paid more money to build dams and reservoirs than they do to tap sub-surface water. Governments would rather build a dam because they can stick a commemorative plaque on it, Dr. Lehr said.
Yet 95 per cent of the available water in the United States is ground water, while only 5 per cent is surface water, he said.
1 would now like to go on to an article from The Toronto Star of May 20, 1985. It is headlined: "Experts doubt U.S. needs our water". I quote from the article which states:
Harvard professor Peter Rogers notes that many cheaper ways exist for the United States to increase its water supply.
The U.S. has about 24 million hectares (60 million acres) of land under irrigation but "could get away with 30 million acres based on exports for the year 2000," saving 50 per cent of the water. And Rogers maintains that wastage is "enormous".

Strong pressure

All of this precious run-off is now washed uselessly away into the sea.
Now we see the political and corporate connections.
Let me turn again to our ambassador for free trade. The January 21, 1986, edition of The Sun of Vancouver says the following:
The export of fresh water from Canada to the U.S. will be a major factor in Canada-U.S. relations, according to Canada's free trade negotiator.
"In my judgment water will be the most critical area of Canada-U.S. relations over the next hundred years," Simon Reisman said in a statement released Monday by communications director Bruce McDonald.
Now we see the historic connections of Mr. Reisman, the Power Corporation and various interests in the United States

February 25, 1986
Water Export and Diversion Act
who do not want to clean up smoke stacks or chemical, toxic and nuclear dumps. 1 think the words of Dr. David Suzuki really hit the nail on the head regarding how these interests all work together. I am quoting from an article which was published in March 1982 which reads as follows:
"Over half of all scientists in the world today are working for the military, and the majority of the remainder works for private industry," he said.
Suzuki pointed out that it was not surprising that most of the benefits of new developments in technology and in science are thus still accruing overwhelmingly to the military and to private industry.
I think Canadians, Americans and people around the world generally recognize that, but when we are talking about NAWAPA, to which I will now turn, and the Grand Canal schemes, I think we can see who intends to line their pockets and for what reasons.
An article run on March 9, 1985, in the Toronto Star was entitled "Preparing to sell Canada dry?"
Is Canada's water for sale? The previous Government said No. Last year, then-environment Minister Charles Caccia said "We reject the notion that water is available for export. This will be a very important commodity in the decades ahead."-
We can't afford to allow water exports, no matter what the price. A firm, simple No is the only thing that can put these grandiose schemes to rest. The Prime Minister should be saying this, not sending a message to foreigners that Canada is for sale.
I certainly agree with that editorial. I turn now to an article contained in The Financial Post of September 5, 1981, entitled "Water crisis trickling into our consciousness". It reads as follows:
This energy-related water demand occurs where there is already short supply (the West), or, in the case of nuclear power, where water quality is already threatened (Ontario). In the U.S., this conflict is compounded by a growing reliance on coal, which not only produces acid rain, but also releases large quantities of carbon dioxide.
It's expected that increasing levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide will raise lower atmosphere temperatures (the "greenhouse" effect) by at least two-five degrees Celsius by the year 2050, thus reducing precipitation.
Since this will aggravate the present drought in much of western North America, the pressure for massive water transfers-and exports from Canada- is likely to increase.
We can see that there are many players in this game. As I have said before, there are the smoke stack industries and those who do not want to clean up these problems like toxic waste and then we deal with who is really going to be making the money and who are the losers. As I will point out in a moment, all the people of the world might well be the losers from either NAWAPA or this lunatic Grand Canal scheme.
The Citizen ran an article on April 28, 1981, entitled "Water supply crisis looms" which reads as follows:
Total Canadian water use is expected to double in the next two decades, from 26.3 billion gallons a day to 62.2 billion gallons daily. Manufacturing and energy needs make the largest demands. Last year, 48 per cent of Canadian water use went to power stations for cooling purposes, while manufacturers drew 32 per cent.
Let us add those two figures together, Mr. Speaker. That amounts to 80 per cent of Canada's water use.
The article continues:
Growth in these areas, particularly as Canada strives for energy self-sufficiency, and agricultural expansion in already water short Western Canada are expected to place the greatest pressures for increased water consumption.
As hewers of wood, we know that we are in a crisis with coal, wood and all of our raw resources. What about us as drawers of water? Those politicians who Say that we are hewers of wood and drawers of water had better understand that these kinds of massive diversions and exports would create a global crisis to which I now turn.
An article entitled "Why U.S. engineers want to turn on Canada's tap" appeared in The Sun of Vancouver in April 1981.
It says the following:
During 1980, Americans used 235.5 billion gallons of fresh water every day. Nearly half of this amount, or 105.2 billion gallons, was not replaced by snow or rainfall. To make up the difference, great underground reservoirs known as aquifers are gradually being tapped for their ancient water supplies. The public is alarmed by reports of "the browning of America."
This is the atmosphere which has given a fresh lease on life to enormous water transfer projects such as that dreamed up in California in 1964 by the huge engineering firm, the Ralph M. Parsons Co. Called the North American Water and Power Alliance, this gigantic project with a price tag of more than $200 billion would bring water from the Yukon down to Mexico.
Let me turn now to our global problems in terms of atmospheric pollution and the implications of such a large diversion project. I am not talking about the impact on migratory birds or the sea life in any of these areas or of the native people and others who would be displaced. I am talking about things on a much larger scale. In an article written by Dr. Kenneth Hare, recognized in this country as being one of our foremost atmospheric scientists, the following appears:
Careful statistical analysis shows not only the 100,000-year interval seemingly favoured by glacial epochs, but also the influence of small changes in the orbit of the sun that recur at intervals of 41,000 and 19,000 to 23,000 years.
These recent discoveries are not yet properly understood, but they are formidable evidence that the "ice age" to which we are alleged to be returning was in fact a succession of glacial epochs spread over two million years or more. Each of these epochs, incidentally, was far longer than the history of civilization!-
Calculations suggest that carbon dioxide will double its atmospheric concentration by mid-21st Century or later. This assumes that the world goes on increasing its use of oil, gas and coal, but that high prices keep the buildup down to about 2 per cent per annum.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-LOCATION OF UNITED STATES NUCLEAR WASTE DUMPS
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-LOCATION OF UNITED STATES NUCLEAR WASTE DUMPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the occasion for my participation this evening in the adjournment debate is the result of a question which I put to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) on January 28, in which 1 expressed concern about the proposed location in the United States of several nuclear waste storage dumps. I understand this evening that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Cook) will be responding. 1 am sure that is of some relief to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Gurbin).
Apparently the United States is examining the possibility of 20 sites in the U.S., several of which are along the American-Canadian border. Thirteen of the sites are in four states bordering Canada. They are located in Minnesota, Wisconsin, New Hampshire and Maine. The rest of the proposed sites are in the southeast section of the states. Of the 13 sites along the Canadian border about which we are expressing concern, eight are of direct concern to Canadian authorities. One site of specific concern is located in Maine.
1 appreciate that the Minister of the Environment, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) have made strong representations to the Government of the United States and to officials of the environment agency to ensure that every protection is given to the environment in Canada. However, I think it is important to register now our objection to the potential location of any of those sites along the Canadian border. Specifically I want to refer to the potential prospects of the site in Maine. That site is in the River Ste. Croix watershed area which creates the border, in part, between the State of Maine and the Province of New Brunswick. The actual site itself would be located, if it became a reality, within 40 miles of the border. Of course the concern is that watersheds and other ecologically critical and sensitive areas could be adversely affected.
It is well known that Maine's geological history indicates that there are no safe places in the State of Maine for the safe storage of nuclear waste. Although we recognize that most other areas which are under consideration in the United States have the same difficulties, the Maine site is a good example for us to utilize when we are examining the potential impact and damages that could accrue to Canada, particularly to the Province of New Brunswick, as a result.
Adjournment Debate
I hope that I have reinforced what the Minister of the Environment has already responded to me for the assurance of the citizens of those areas which could be affected. The Canadian Government will indeed continue to monitor very closely these proposals to store nuclear radioactive wastes in storage dumps along the Canadian border. We will continue to impress upon our U.S. counterparts that the establishment of these nuclear waste dumps in our area, where potentially dangerous environmental impact could be felt, is unacceptable to Canadians. It is unacceptable to endanger our environment to that extent and we will use evry influence available to us to ensure that when those sites are selected, if that method of disposal is indeed decided upon, they will not be in proximity of the Canadian border to the satisfaction of the Canadian Government and to the relief of the concerns of those who are extremely perplexed about the consequences to the environmentally sensitive areas on our side of the U.S.-Canadian border.

speakeroldname: Mr. Chuck Cook (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-LOCATION OF UNITED STATES NUCLEAR WASTE DUMPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) has raised a question which could be of concern to all Canadians. I am delighted to have the opportunity to rise this evening to give him complete, solid, and total relief from his concern.
The U.S. nuclear waste repository program, which is searching for a site for its second repository, has caused concern. Canada has insisted from the start that any site selected for a U.S. nuclear waste repository must pose no threat to the Canadian environment or to the health of this or future generations of Canadians.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has discussed this issue several times with United States Secretary of State George Shultz. Last spring they established Canada-U.S. consultative meetings to ensure that there would be a well-defined process by which Canadian concerns could be addressed and resolved with the United States. Federal officials have benefited in this consultative process from the views and concerns of provincial experts as well.
In addition to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) have discussed the issue with their U.S. counterparts. These discussions have resulted in the firm U.S. commitment to consult with Canada throughout the entire U.S. program. Most significantly, the U.S. has promised that it will drop from consideration any potential area that could require field work in Canada.
In a letter to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the U.S. State Department pledged that the 15-year U.S. Department of Energy screening process is intended to ensure that no site will be selected which will have harmful effects on either side of the border.
During the last year, the United States looked at 235 areas for a potential site for the second repository. Approximately 40

February 25, 1986
Adjournment Debate
of these were within 25 miles of the Canada-U.S. border from New Brunswick to Manitoba. The U.S. Department of Energy draft report issued on January 16, 1986, narrowed the number of areas under consideration to 20, none of which is within 25 miles of Canada. One site along the Maine-Quebec border was specifically dropped from the report as it would have required field work in Canada.
A number of the 20 areas identified in the recent U.S. report may present concerns to Canada as they are all or partially in watersheds that flow into Canada, or are very close to such watersheds. The Provinces of New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, and Manitoba have been provided with copies of the report and the federal Government has already met with them once since the report was issued, and will meet with them again before the next Canada-U.S. consultative meeting, which will likely take place sometime in April.
Following the release by the U.S. of the report in its final form in July, the 20 areas identified will be subject to field investigations leading to a narrowing to three areas in 1991. These three areas will then be subject to intensive research leading to a final selection of one site in 1998. Throughout this elaborate process the Canadian Government will follow developments closely and will ensure, by every possible means, that the one site eventually selected will pose no risk whatsoever to the Canadian environment or to the health of this or future generations of Canadians.
I sincerely hope that answer will relieve the mind of the Member for Fundy-Royal.

subtopic: FORESTRY-VANCOUVER ISLAND FOREST LANDS. (B) REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL FUNDING
FORESTRY-VANCOUVER ISLAND FOREST LANDS. (B) REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over a year ago I asked the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) about long-term federal funding for forestry on Vancouver Island. This has been a long-term concern of both myself and my Party, but the immediate stimulus for my question was the proposal by the Vancouver Island Mayors called "Strategy for Survival". I am very pleased that the Minister is present in the House this evening to give a direct response to my concerns. I know he endorses the concept contained in this proposal. The problem does not lie so much with the Minister as it does with the present Government's priorities.
The Minister's response to my question was basically: Wait and see. We have waited for over a year now and we have not seen the kind of funding which is needed if Vancouver Island is going to recover from the present recession. I just want to draw the attention of the Minister to the fact that there are fewer people working on Vancouver Island today than there were when his Government was elected in September, 1984. According to Statistics Canada, in January, 1986, we had
187.000	people working on Vancouver Island. In September of 1984 the figure was 207,000 people. That adds up to a loss of
20.000	jobs while this Government has been in office. We are concerned that, while the Government seems to be creating
jobs in other parts of Canada, it is not creating jobs on Vancouver Island.
Last June the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry heard testimony from the Vancouver Island Mayors who had originally put forward this proposal "Strategy for Survival". The proposal documents the economic benefits which would be gained from investment in intensive forestry on Vancouver Island. I am sure the Minister would agree that this is among the best forest land in Canada, indeed anywhere in the world. The federal-provincial forestry agreement emphasizes reforestation in areas of British Columbia which have not yet been satisfactorily restocked. As the Minister knows, reforestation is not the major problem on Vancouver Island. The problem is how to make the best and most intensive use of this prime forest land.
The Mayors' proposal points out that for an investment of some $22.3 million a year in an ongoing program, some 1,100 direct and 500 indirect jobs would be created. Over the 45-year life of this kind of program, the Mayors suggest that the harvestable volume of wood would increase by 33 per cent. The total value would increase by 55 per cent, which amounts to some $655 million. The revenue return to the Government would increase by 33 per cent or some $79 million. The value of this kind of program is not the subject of debate this evening. There might be some quibbles one way or another about some of the fine points, but I am sure the Minister himself agrees with the basic value of this kind of investment. In fact, he has endorsed the principle involved. What is at issue is the question of federal funding.
On June 28 the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry endorsed the proposal and the sixth report made to this Parliament unanimously called for the federal Government to give favourable consideration to funding.
On September 16 the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) moved that the House concur in the committee report. Unfortunately this motion was talked out by Conservative back-benchers who did not want the issue to come to a vote. They knew it would have passed and that would have given a clear signal to the Government that it should give this kind of program very high priority. Government back-benchers said that we were rushing things. The Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg) said that he had been talking to the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) and that they had been very encouraging. He said, as recorded at page 6650 of Hansard for September 16, 1985, and I quote:
If you can put your ear to the railway and listen for what is coming, I anticipate that it will be a favourable response and I will be quite happy when that happens-
We have been waiting for that favourable response for a long time and it still has not happened. We have had instead a patchwork approach to forestry in the form of funding through Section 38. We appreciate that kind of funding, but it has
February 25, 1986

meant that sometimes we have had inappropriate priorities. It is like buying groceries at the corner convenience store instead of doing a proper shopping trip with a list and buying things in order. You pay too great a price for start-up and shut-down when you are dealing in this kind of patchwork manner with forestry projects.
We do not need to fixate on the particular program of the mayors. We can look at other mechanisms, but what we do need is some commitment of funding to forestry on Vancouver Island. We know that there are problems with protectionist pressure from the United States in lumber.

Member that of the funds under the agreement and under the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), a large amount of money has been and will be spent on Vancouver Island to help redress the unemployment situation. sheer size of that one small area but nonetheless important area of Canada. subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-THREAT OF PRE-CHRISTMAS STRIKE
CANADA POST CORPORATION-THREAT OF PRE-CHRISTMAS STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several weeks ago I asked the Minister responsible for Canada Post about the possibility of the Government giving serious consideration to outlawing strikes at Canada Post. I suggest that a poll would show that a very high proportion of Canadians are very dissatisfied with the over-all delivery service of Canada Post and would want to declare that service essential to prevent employees from striking.
The new President was appointed recently. We welcome the news that Mr. Donald Lander is now the top Chief Executive Officer. I wish him well because he has an awesome task to undertake on behalf of all Canadians.
Let me dwell on some examples from my riding of Don Valley East concerning the level of service we are experiencing. Today I received a letter from a Mr. Mariano DiGangi who enclosed an envelope posted in downtown Toronto on January 31, 1986 which he just received yesterday, February 19. He asks: "Should it take 20 days for a letter to travel less than 15 miles?" He states that the letter contained a cheque but who will repay him for the lost interest on the sum it represented? He states: "When will we insist on performance standards appropriate to the rising costs of postal service in this country?"
Yesterday, I was on the phone to Mrs. Jane Hunter at apartment 203, 4003 Bayview Avenue. There are three large apartment buildings at this location, housing many senior citizens who receive pension cheques. Until about two months ago they regularly received their mail at two o'clock in the afternoon. For the last several weeks they have had no idea when the mail would arrive-arriving as late as 9:30 in the evening. I recently spoke to the postal authority about this case. They are supposed to remeasure the burden of that route and advise us shortly.
There are many horror stories. A good friend of mine received a letter from Korea in four days. It was a special

February 25, 1986
Adjournment Debate
delivery letter, costing $55 Canadian, but it only took four days to come from Korea to downtown Toronto. However, it took six days for that letter to go from downtown Toronto to Willowdale. That is totally unacceptable.
Another example is the constituent who sent in a copy of an envelope which was mailed from his bank. It took six days to get from the Toronto Dominion Bank on Bayview Avenue to one block away. I applaud the former Minister responsible for Canada Post. He launched the Marchment Committee. I believe that group did an excellent job in travelling across Canada to find out about the various issues. It came up with 43 separate recommendations. I sincerely hope that the new president and his management will study those recommendations very thoroughly and give each and every one serious consideration.
I would like to touch on a few of the major items in the report. Of course, we all know of the massive deficit that Crown corporation-which was just set up three years ago-is enduring. Very recently we had to pour another $243 million of taxpayers' money into that company. In the Marchment report there is a major recommendation in which targets are really set. All Canadians require a postal service which they can depend on for reliable first-class and second-class mail. It should be consistent and dependable. The report then went on to set up a three-tiered target system which states that mail should take no longer than two days to be delivered within a given city from the time it is mailed, it should take no longer than three days within a province and no longer than four days anywhere in Canada.
Obviously, in a great many examples, we are missing those targets by a country mile, but I hope the new president and his management team will get down to brass tacks in terms of increased productivity and dependability of service.
We can hit upon certain ironies in that organization with respect to its set-up right now. Most mail gets sorted at night, yet the men and women with the most experience work during the day, so the most inexperienced people are trying to handle the high volume of mail in the evenings. Delivery carriers are currently paid, I understand, about $12.98 an hour. They receive time and a half for the first two hours of overtime and double time for any hours over that. I worked out an example. If one of them worked until nine o'clock on a given day, he would receive for the first two hours of overtime $38.94, an additional $103.84, for those other four hours and if we add in his regular seven or eight hour day-and I am using seven hours-of $90.86 the total gross pay for that one day alone, excluding benefits, would be $233.74, this has been going on for many weeks and I suspect it is related to low productivity and just too many days off. The average employee of Canada Post has 18 days off a year. That is double the average of the private sector. It is almost an extra month off. Most months have about 21 working days.
This is such a serious subject and such an awesome task, as I mentioned, for Mr. Lander to tackle, that I would like to quote from an article in today's Toronto Sun by Laura Sabia:
A case can be made that the post office is an essential service. Outlaw strikes and replace them with hard-nosed negotiations. We can no longer carry the baggage of intimidation by threats of strike. We can no longer permit problems to increase and fester. A stern but fair policy is needed, enunciated loud and clear by government and executed by the new president. If we must face confrontation with the unions, let's face it now and erase the slate clean.
There are some 60,000 employees in that organization. Obviously, thousands of them are well meaning, hard-working people. Clearly we have some very severe problems with the union side and with management, I underscore, and I, for one-and I know I speak on behalf of thousands of Canadians-wish Mr. Lander well. 1 wish him Godspeed and good luck in getting that organization turned around so that it will not only give good service but it will make a profit as do the post offices in the United States and in Australia.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Domm (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Canada Post):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-THREAT OF PRE-CHRISTMAS STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the limited time available to me I will deal with the subject matter of the Hon. Member's question which was first raised on November 7, 1985. At that time intense negotiations were going on with the Union of Postal Communications Employees which represents some 4,000 employees at Canada Post.
The Minister expressed optimism at that time that both parties would arrive at a negotiated settlement. I am happy to report that that turned out to be the case as far as the Union of Postal Communications Employees is concerned.
At this very moment members of the union are in the process of ratifying a tentative agreement reached two weeks ago with the assistance of a conciliation commissioner appointed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight). When this tentative agreement is signed in a few weeks, Canada Post will have completed an entire round of negotiations with all nine of its unions, which represents some 29 bargaining units, without any strikes having occurred.
What this illustrates is that we have a corporation and its unions which have reached the maturity to settle their differences at a negotiating table and not on picket lines. This successful round of negotiations also indicates that the laws governing labour relations in Canada really work and that the structures in place to ensure fair labour settlements and justice in the workplace are effective in achieving these objectives.
When Canada Post became a Crown corporation almost five years ago, one of the key issues was to shift the jurisdiction governing labour relations from the Public Service Staff Relations Act to the Canada Labour Code. There have not been any strikes at Canada Post for the past four years. This situation is the consequence of the flexibility that the Canada Labour Code provides for both parties to reach a negotiated settlement. The series of collective agreements reached with all of Canada Post's unions in this first round of negotiations under the Canada Labour Code is positive proof that the system is working.
February 25, 1986

With respect to strikes being made illegal at Canada Post, I feel confident that the matter should be left under the jurisdiction of the Canada Labour Code. We should continue to negotiate satisfactorily at the bargaining table contracts between the 29 unions represented at Canada Post.
